title: 8 Ways to Stop the Thumb Sucking Habit
summary: A gentle, 8-step pediatrician's plan to help your child stop thumb sucking, plus when bite changes matter and when to see your dentist.
body_text: Title Tag: How to Stop Thumb Sucking: A Pediatrician's Guide Meta Description: A gentle, 8-step pediatrician's plan to help your child stop thumb sucking, plus when bite changes matter and when to see your dentist. Thumb sucking is one of the most common worries parents bring up at well-child visits. The good news is that for most children, it is a normal, self-soothing reflex that fades on its own. This guide helps you tell the difference between a habit you can leave alone and one worth working on, with a step-by-step plan that uses kindness, not punishment. Quick answer: Most children stop thumb sucking on their own between ages 2 and 4. If the habit is still strong past age 3, or you notice changes in the front teeth or the roof of the mouth, talk to your pediatrician or pediatric dentist. The most effective plan gets your child on board, rewards thumb-free time, uses gentle reminders, and brings in a clinician if needed. Key Takeaways Thumb sucking is developmentally normal in babies and toddlers, and most children stop on their own between ages 2 and 4. Active treatment is rarely needed before about age 4. Strong, frequent sucking past ages 2 to 4 can start to affect how the front teeth and roof of the mouth line up. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) suggests a dental visit if the habit continues past age 3. Lasting bite changes become more likely once the permanent front teeth come in, around ages 5 to 6. If your child stops before then, the bite often corrects itself. The most effective approach is positive: get your child's buy-in, reward thumb-free time, watch for triggers, and use gentle reminders. Punishment and shaming tend to backfire. About 1 in 25 children are still sucking at age 8, and roughly 1 in 50 at age 12, so most kids outgrow the habit with time. How to Stop Thumb Sucking: 8 Gentle Steps If you are looking for a quick plan, start here. Each step is explained in more detail below. Wait and reassure if your child is under about age 4. No active treatment is needed before age 2. Between 2 and 4, mild discouragement is plenty for most kids. Get your child on board. Children stop fastest when they want to. Ask if they would like to work on it, and let them help pick the plan. Ignore the habit if it seems attention seeking. For some children, no reaction at all is enough. Reward thumb-free time. Praise small wins. A sticker chart, a calendar, or a small daily prize works well for preschoolers. Spot the triggers. Watch for boredom, tiredness, and stress. Offer a hug, a fidget toy, or something to do with the hands. Use gentle nighttime reminders. A loose sock or soft mitten over the hand, an adhesive bandage on the thumb, or a bitter-tasting nail coating can be a reminder, not a punishment. Skip punishment, shaming, and nagging. They tend to make the habit last longer. Loop in your pediatrician or pediatric dentist if the habit continues past age 3, if it is intense or constant, or if you notice changes in the front teeth or the roof of the mouth. Why Kids Suck Their Thumbs Sucking on a thumb, finger, or pacifier is what doctors call non-nutritive sucking. It is a built-in reflex that helps babies calm themselves, fall asleep, and feel safe. One large review found up to 8 in 10 infants do it in the first few months of life. About 7 in 10 children ages 2 to 5 still suck at least sometimes. The habit fades for most children between ages 2 and 4. By age 8, only about 4 in 100 children still suck their thumb. If your toddler still sucks her thumb at nap time, she is in good company, and there is a strong chance she will stop on her own. When Thumb Sucking Becomes a Dental Concern This is the part parents most often want a clear answer to. There is no single magic age, but pediatric and dental groups agree on a useful framework. Short answer: most children stop on their own before the permanent front teeth come in (around ages 5 to 6), and a habit that is still strong past age 3 is the main signal to loop in a pediatric dentist. Age What to know Source Under 2 Do not try to stop the habit. Sucking is a normal comfort and usually will not damage the teeth at this age. Mayo Clinic Past ages 2 to 4 (strong, frequent sucking) The habit may start to affect the shape of the mouth or how the teeth line up. AAP / HealthyChildren Continues past age 3 The AAPD recommends a dental check and gentle, active discouragement. AAPD Permanent front teeth coming in (about ages 5 to 6) The risk of lasting changes to the teeth and palate goes up. Mayo Clinic Stops before permanent teeth The bite often corrects itself. AAP / HealthyChildren In plain language: the older the child and the more intense the sucking, the more it matters. The single biggest predictor of lasting change is whether the habit is still strong once the permanent front teeth come in. "If your child stops sucking on their thumb or fingers before their permanent front teeth come in, there's a good chance their bite will correct itself." American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org What Thumb Sucking Can Do to the Teeth and Mouth When the habit is long and strong, the most common dental effects are: Anterior open bite. The front teeth do not meet when the back teeth are closed. Increased overjet. The top front teeth stick out past the bottom ones. Posterior crossbite. The upper back teeth fit inside the lower back teeth on one or both sides, often linked to a narrower upper jaw. Studies have found that children with a long thumb or finger habit have about a 4 times higher risk of bite problems compared with children who did not suck. Finger and thumb habits are also linked to bigger changes than pacifier use. A few other notes worth knowing: Skin and nails. A long, intense habit can lead to thick, dry skin on the thumb, nail changes, or a small infection at the nail fold. These usually go away once the habit stops. Speech. Older articles sometimes claim thumb sucking causes specific speech problems. Recent reviews do not strongly support that. There may be a link in some children, but it is not certain. A Closer Look at the Plan A few of the steps above are worth a little extra context. Get your child on board. This is the biggest single predictor of success. Talk to your child in plain words. Ask what they think about thumb sucking and whether they would like to work on it. Children who feel they chose to stop do far better than children who feel pushed. Reward thumb-free time. Keep goals small at first. "No sucking during dinner" or "no sucking during one bedtime story" is easier to win than a whole day. A sticker chart or a calendar with stars works well for preschoolers. Build up from short wins. Spot the triggers. Watch when the thumb goes in. Boredom, tiredness, hunger, screen time, and stressful moments are the common ones. Offer a fidget toy, a snack, a hug, or a task that needs both hands. For older kids, target the underlying feeling, not just the thumb. Use gentle nighttime reminders. Many kids suck most during sleep . A loose sock or soft mitten, an adhesive bandage on the thumb, or a bitter-tasting nail coating can serve as a reminder. Talk about it with your child first so it feels like teamwork, not a trap. Skip punishment. The AAP and the AAPD both note that scolding or shaming children for thumb sucking tends to prolong it. It can also create power struggles. If you feel like you are nagging, take a step back. Worried about your child's thumb sucking? Talk to a Blueberry pediatrician What About Appliances and Special Devices? For older children with a stubborn habit and clear bite changes, a pediatric dentist may suggest a small mouth appliance such as a palatal crib or palatal arch. These sit behind the upper front teeth and make thumb sucking less satisfying. A 2015 Cochrane review of 6 small studies found that both mouth appliances and reward-based programs helped more children stop than no treatment. Palatal cribs worked slightly better than palatal arches. The studies were small, though, so the overall quality of the evidence is low. Barrier methods alone, such as gloves or bitter coatings, often are not enough for a long-standing habit. For parents: an appliance can be a useful tool for older kids, but it works best as part of a plan that also includes your child's motivation and rewards. Talk it through with your child's dentist before deciding. When to Call Your Pediatrician or Dentist When to get a professional eye on it Call your pediatrician or pediatric dentist if your child is still sucking strongly past age 3, if you see an open bite or change in the roof of the mouth, if the skin on the thumb is cracked, bleeding, or infected, or if the habit seems tied to anxiety, stress, or another behavior change. At Blueberry Pediatrics, families can reach a pediatrician by message, phone, or video to talk through a thumb sucking plan, check on bite changes, or get a referral to a pediatric dentist. In our telehealth visits, the most common question parents bring up is whether a 3- or 4-year-old has waited too long to break the habit. The honest answer is almost always no, especially when the sucking is fading from constant to mostly nap time and sleep. Frequently Asked Questions At what age should my child stop sucking their thumb? Most children stop on their own between ages 2 and 4. Pediatric dentists usually recommend a check if the habit continues past age 3, and the risk of lasting bite changes rises once the permanent front teeth come in, around ages 5 to 6. Does thumb sucking really hurt the teeth? It can, but only when it is frequent, strong, and continues into the years when the permanent teeth come in. Mild, occasional sucking in a toddler is usually not a dental problem. Is pacifier use better or worse than thumb sucking? The dental effects look similar at younger ages, but a pacifier is easier to retire than a thumb. Studies also suggest finger and thumb habits are linked to bigger bite changes than pacifier use when the habit lasts a long time. What if my child only sucks at night? Nighttime sucking is the hardest piece to break because it happens in sleep. A soft mitten, a loose sock, or a bitter nail coating, paired with rewards for thumb-free mornings, often helps. Does thumb sucking cause speech problems? Older articles sometimes say yes, but recent reviews do not strongly support a direct cause. If your child has a speech delay, talk to your pediatrician about a speech evaluation rather than blaming the thumb. A Final Word Thumb sucking is one of the most common and most outgrown habits in childhood. For most children, kindness, patience, and a few small tools are enough. If your child needs more help, your pediatrician and pediatric dentist are on your team. Still not sure how to help your child stop? title: How Automation Improves Local Government Efficiency
summary: Local governments are under growing pressure to do more with limited staff and resources. AI and automation can improve efficiency, but their greatest value often extends beyond reducing manual work. When implemented thoughtfully, automation changes how information moves across an organization, helping departments make faster decisions, collaborate more effectively, and spend less time waiting for information. Pickens County, Georgia, saw those benefits after modernizing its finance...
body_text: How Automation Improves Local Government Efficiency August 04, 2026 by Amber Ventimiglia Local governments are under growing pressure to do more with limited staff and resources. AI and automation can improve efficiency, but their greatest value often extends beyond reducing manual work. When implemented thoughtfully, automation changes how information moves across an organization, helping departments make faster decisions, collaborate more effectively, and spend less time waiting for information. Pickens County, Georgia , saw those benefits after modernizing its finance operations with AI-assisted invoice capture and accounts payable (AP) automation. Previously, the county relied on separate applications that didn’t communicate with one another. Finance could see where work stood, but other departments couldn’t. Staff often waited for monthly reports or contacted the finance team for updates before making routine purchasing and budgeting decisions. Many local governments evaluate automation by asking one question: How much manual work does it eliminate? Pickens County suggests a better one: How much organizational friction does it remove? Automation Does More Than Eliminate Manual Work Like many local governments, Pickens County’s accounts payable process depended heavily on manual effort. Invoice information was entered by hand, departments lacked real-time visibility into financial data, and finance staff spent valuable time answering status questions instead of focusing on financial management. AI-assisted invoice capture simplified that workflow. Instead of manually entering invoice data, staff could upload invoices directly into the system, where AI extracted much of the information automatically before routing invoices through the approval process. The AP automation system has empowered them to complete disbursements in batches of 60-100 at once. As Accounts Payable Specialist Hollie Poole explained, “I just grab your invoice off my email and throw it in the capture ... It’s really a huge efficiency time saver. We love it.” Reducing manual data entry certainly saved time. But it also made the entire approval process more transparent. Build Efficiency That Scales Learn how agencies improve efficiency by expanding capacity through connected systems, data, and workflows. Shared Visibility Accelerates Decisions Once invoices entered the automated workflow, departments could see where they were in the approval process without contacting finance. Managers could monitor budgets through scheduled reports and dashboards rather than waiting for monthly updates, helping them identify issues sooner. For Poole, that visibility fundamentally changed day-to-day operations. “At any moment, there’s not a question of, ‘Where’s that invoice?’ or 'Who’s supposed to be looking at that?’” That shared visibility eliminates countless small interruptions that slow work across local government. Instead of sifting through emails, checking multiple systems, or asking another department for updates, employees spend more time moving work forward. When automation reduces organizational waiting time, decisions happen faster. Efficiency Grows When Information Moves Freely As AI and automation continue to evolve, local governments will have even more opportunities to streamline routine work. But technology delivers its greatest value when it improves how departments work together — not simply how quickly they complete individual tasks. Pickens County’s experience demonstrates that lesson well. AI-assisted automation reduced manual effort, but the broader outcome was a more connected financial operation where information was easier to access, approvals moved faster, accountability improved, and departments could make decisions with greater confidence. For local government leaders, that larger shift is valuable. Sustainable efficiency comes from ensuring the right people have the right information at the right time. By removing delays between people, information, and decisions, AI-assisted automation helps organizations move work forward with greater confidence. Work moves faster because the organization moves together. About the Author Amber Ventimiglia Amber Ventimiglia is vice president and general manager of Tyler Technologies’ small- and mid-size local government ERP solutions business. She oversees strategy and operations to help local governments streamline operations, improve efficiency, and deliver better outcomes for residents, with a particular focus on helping small towns thrive. title: Digital asset fund manager survey - august 2026
summary: Digital asset allocations rise to 1.2%, driven entirely by institutions. Volatility remains the top barrier, while bitcoin retains the most compelling growth outlook.
body_text: Home Insights Research & data Digital asset fund manager survey - august 2026 4 min read The first step back In Allocations rose to 1.2%, the first increase since the October 2025 sell-off, driven entirely by institutions rotating out of fixed income and commodities. Value perception was the fastest-rising reason to invest. Volatility is the leading barrier for the uninvested, despite 30-day volatility sitting near its record low of 22%. Investors are pricing drawdown risk, not realised volatility. Regulation remains the top concern among the invested, reflecting Clarity Act uncertainty, though corporate restrictions and regulatory fears have fallen sharply among those yet to invest. Bitcoin retains the most compelling growth outlook. Ether's has deteriorated sharply on Clarity Act delays and senior staff turnover at the Ethereum Foundation, with modest rotation into altcoins. Bitcoin retains the top spot as the digital asset with the most compelling growth outlook, little changed from last quarter. The outlook for ether has deteriorated sharply, which we believe reflects the falling odds of the Clarity Act passing this year alongside concerns over the high turnover of senior staff at the Ethereum Foundation. Most altcoins were little changed. The exception was the "other" category, which saw the largest rise of any component, with respondents citing Zcash, HYPE and SUI. Digital asset allocations rose to 1.2% of portfolios, the first increase since the sell-off began in October 2025, suggesting investors are beginning to re-allocate. Across cohorts, the move was driven entirely by institutional investors. Institutions have also rotated into other higher-risk asset classes, notably equities, funding this by selling commodities and fixed income. Bitcoin and ether remain the core holdings in portfolios, although we have seen a reduction in those positions in favour of altcoins. This surprises us given the poor sentiment of the past quarter, which typically weighs more heavily on altcoins. The data suggests multi-asset approaches in particular have gained in popularity. This hasn’t been reflected in fund flow data. Diversification and client demand remain the primary motivations for investing, together accounting for 50% of the rationale for adding digital assets to portfolios. Appetite for exposure to distributed ledger technology has also risen modestly. The most notable increase, however, was in investors' perception of the asset class as good value. This is encouraging, and suggests recent price weakness is being read as a buying opportunity rather than a warning. Volatility has risen to the top of the list of reasons preventing investors from buying digital assets. We believe the perception of price movements over the past quarter is the main culprit, despite 30-day volatility currently sitting close to its record low of 22%. Reputational risk remains another stubborn barrier to entry. More encouragingly, corporate restrictions and concerns over regulation have both fallen sharply, presumably reflecting the proliferation of ETPs and continued constructive regulatory progress. Regulation remains the top concern among those already invested. This doesn't surprise us, given the ongoing uncertainty surrounding the Clarity Act. Volatility has fallen, yet it remains a persistent concern, perhaps because investors are responding to bitcoin's drawdown risk rather than its realised volatility. Quantum risk continues to come up in client meetings, which likely explains why so many selected it. There has been a sharp rise in the share of investors who believe the Fed is making a policy mistake. The survey doesn't distinguish between whether respondents think the Fed is too hawkish or too dovish, but a considerable number moved from undecided to yes. ABOUT OUR SURVEY: The July 2026 Survey drew 30 responses from investors who cover ~US$1.16 trillion of assets under management. Published on Aug 19th, 2026 Writer James Butterfill Head of Research Former Head of Research at ETF Securities, James leads CoinShares' Research department with deep expertise in equity and fund management.
