title: Intelligent Spam Lead Filtering
summary: Surface now filters spam submissions automatically before they reach your CRM or trigger any workflows.
body_text: Surface now filters spam submissions automatically before they reach your CRM or trigger any workflows. The Problem Anyone who's run inbound forms for more than a few months knows the pattern. You check your CRM in the morning and find a handful of submissions from the previous day that are clearly junk — asdfasdf@mailinator.com , someone who submitted the same form six times in a row, a "company name" field that just says "test." The issue isn't just that junk submissions exist. It's what happens downstream. They get routed to reps, trigger nurture sequences, inflate your lead counts, and take up paid seats in your CRM. Most teams deal with this reactively — manually deleting bad records, building Zapier filters, or asking SDRs to eyeball every submission. None of that scales, and all of it happens after the junk has already entered your system. We kept hearing this from Surface customers, so we built spam filtering directly into the submission pipeline. What It Does The core idea is straightforward: validate every submission at the moment it happens, before it gets written to your CRM or triggers any downstream workflows. Here's what runs on each submission: Email validation. Surface checks every email as it's entered — verifying the domain exists, the format is valid, and it's not from a disposable provider like Mailinator or TempMail. Invalid emails are blocked instantly and the prospect is prompted for a work email. Pattern detection. If the same email submits 10 forms in a minute, or we see a burst of identical entries from the same IP, it gets blocked or flagged automatically. Content screening. Obvious test data in form fields — "test test test", "asdf", single-character entries — gets flagged for review rather than passed to your sales team. Quarantine, not deletion. Nothing is permanently thrown away. Blocked submissions go to a quarantine view where you can review them and recover false positives. What It Catches Type Example Handling Disposable email domains user@mailinator.com , name@tempmail.org Blocked; prospect prompted for work email Non-existent domains name@fakecorp.xyz Blocked at submission Rapid repeated submissions Same email, 10 submissions in 1 minute Auto-blocked Test/junk field data "test test test", "asdf", "xxx" Flagged for review Bot patterns Auto-generated strings, keyword stuffing Quarantined Sequential test entries test1@co.com , test2@co.com , test3@co.com Flagged as suspicious How It Fits Into the Rest of Surface Spam filtering runs as the first step in Surface's submission pipeline, before lead scoring, enrichment, or routing. The sequence looks like this: Prospect submits a form Spam filter validates the submission — blocks, flags, or passes it Clean submissions proceed to enrichment (company data, firmographics, etc.) Lead scoring evaluates fit and intent Routing assigns the lead to the right rep or workflow This ordering matters. If spam gets through to step 3, you're burning enrichment credits on junk data. If it reaches step 5, a rep wastes time on it. Filtering at step 2 means everything downstream operates on clean data. For existing Surface customers, this doesn't require rebuilding your workflows. Spam filtering slots in automatically — just enable it and optionally configure your domain allowlists/blocklists. Configuration Out of the box, spam filtering works without any setup. The default settings block disposable email providers and flag obvious test data. If you want to customize: Domain lists. Allowlist specific domains (useful if you have partners on unusual domains that might get flagged) or blocklist domains you know are problematic. Free email handling. By default, Surface allows submissions from Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook, etc. If you're strictly B2B and only want work emails, you can toggle this to flag or block free email providers. FAQ Does this add latency to the form experience? No. Validation runs in milliseconds. From the prospect's perspective, the form behaves normally unless their email gets flagged, in which case they see an inline message asking for a work email. What if a real lead gets blocked? Blocked submissions appear in the quarantine view. You can recover any submission with one click and it'll flow through to your CRM as if it had passed normally. Over time you can tune your allowlists to reduce false positives. Is this on by default for new accounts? Yes. New Surface accounts have spam filtering enabled with default settings. You can disable it or customize it from the settings panel. Can I see what's being filtered? Yes. The quarantine view shows every blocked and flagged submission, with the reason it was caught. You can also see aggregate stats — how many submissions were filtered over a given period, what the most common spam patterns are, etc.

title: The best 6sense alternatives in 2026
summary: 6sense scores accounts and buys ads, but the outreach is a separate job. The best alternatives run ABM with the execution built in.
body_text: The best 6sense alternative is Artisan, because it runs enterprise account-based marketing (ABM) with the outreach built in instead of treating it as a separate job. 6sense is a powerful predictive ABM suite for scoring accounts and running ads, but it tells you who to target and largely leaves the reaching-out to your team and tools. Demandbase, Bombora, and Common Room own real slices of the category. How the 6sense alternatives compare Rank Tool Best for Standout capability Public pricing 1 Artisan Enterprise ABM with the outreach executed, not just scored Account targeting plus autonomous multichannel outreach in one platform Usage-based credits for Ava's work, dialer seats billed separately ( pricing ) 2 Demandbase Full-stack predictive ABM with advertising Account intelligence plus ad and sales orchestration ~$24K-165K/yr, median ~$68K (Vendr-reported) 3 Bombora Topic-intent data feeding your own stack Company Surge topic intent co-op $25K-100K/yr contracts 4 Common Room Community and product-signal intelligence Cross-source signal capture and person-level stitching $2,500/mo entry 5 ZoomInfo Intent Intent inside a large B2B data platform Scoops and intent tied to deep contact data Add-on to ZoomInfo (from around $15K/yr reported) 6 G2 Buyer Intent Catching in-market software buyers on review pages Signals from buyers researching on the review site Custom within G2 Marketing Solutions (commonly low-to-mid five figures/yr) Why do people look for a 6sense alternative? Three reasons come up repeatedly: cost, complexity, and the execution gap. On cost, 6sense contracts are reported around a $62,820 median and reach past $100K (Vendr-attributed), which is a serious line item before you have sent a single message. On complexity, buyers describe long implementations and the need for a dedicated RevOps or ABM team to configure models, maintain account lists, and translate scores into action. The platform is powerful, and this power has a staffing cost. For the numbers, see 6sense pricing and reviews . The execution gap is the one that catches teams by surprise. 6sense excels at telling you which accounts are in-market and at putting ads in front of them. But the moment you want a human-quality, personalized message to reach a scored contact, you are outside 6sense's core and inside your sequencer, your data tool, and your reps' calendars. The insight is upstream of the work, and the work still has to happen somewhere. For the basics, see what is intent data . None of this means 6sense is a bad platform. It means "ABM" and "outreach" are two jobs, and 6sense mainly owns the first. The alternatives below split roughly into other analytics-heavy suites and one platform that does the targeting and the reaching-out together. For a related play, see how to spot companies creating brand-new roles . What is the best alternative to 6sense? Artisan, if you want enterprise ABM where the outreach is part of the product instead of a downstream project. 6sense hands you a prioritized account list and an ad audience. Artisan builds the list, watches the signals, identifies the visitors, and has Ava run the personalized outreach to the right people at those accounts. Below, Artisan first, then five genuine alternatives. 1. Artisan: Enterprise ABM with the outreach built in Artisan is an AI-first outbound platform built around Ava, an autonomous AI BDR , and it runs account-based motion end to end. You define named-account lists and ideal customer profile (ICP) criteria; Ava watches the signals that predict buying, funding rounds, newly hired executives, first hire in a department, active hiring for a role, tech-stack intent, and Bombora-powered topic intent (the same co-op much of the ABM category resells, said plainly). She identifies visitors from those accounts at the person level on US traffic and company-level globally on a 3.7B-IP graph at a published 92% accuracy rate. Then she does the part 6sense leaves to you: researches the contact, writes a message specific to that person, and sends it across email, social media, and the dialer. For a related play, see Champion tracking: catch past buyers when they change jobs . This is the category-strength point. ABM is not something Artisan hands to a specialist and returns to; it owns the targeting layer and the execution layer in one place. Over 90% of Artisan customers run Ava autonomously, on a dial from review-and-approve to fully autonomous, with plain-language escalation rules and a full audit trail sales ops can govern centrally. The consolidation is the argument against an analytics suite plus a sequencer plus a data platform plus an ops team to wire them together. For how the two approaches compare, see our guide to the best AI GTM platforms . SaaStr's Amelia Lerutte, Chief AI Officer, put it directly: "Email has always been our number one driver. Artisan is now neck-and-neck in both output and closed-won revenue." Their team sent 6,892 emails at a 3.6% positive response rate in roughly six weeks, with 49.4% of social media connection requests accepted. This is ABM where the scoring and the sending live in the same system. Best for: enterprise and mid-market teams that want account targeting and personalized outreach in one governed platform, run centrally by ops. Who should pick something else: a team that only wants a predictive-scoring and advertising layer to feed an existing, heavily built outreach machine, and does not want the execution consolidated. Pricing: Ava's work runs on usage-based credits, dialer seats and phone numbers are billed separately, and there is a free trial. See artisan.co/pricing . 2. Demandbase: The full-stack ABM rival Demandbase is 6sense's closest peer: predictive account intelligence, intent, and advertising orchestration in one suite, with contracts reported from roughly $24K to $165K per year, median around $68K (Vendr-attributed). For teams that want a mature ABM platform with strong advertising and account analytics, it is the direct alternative to evaluate against 6sense head to head. It shares 6sense's shape, though. It is analytics-and-ads-heavy, and the personalized outreach to scored accounts is still a separate execution layer. Best for: enterprises that want a full-stack ABM and advertising suite as an alternative to 6sense. Who should pick something else: teams that want the outreach executed inside the platform instead of orchestrated to reps and ads. Pricing: ~$24K-165K/yr, median ~$68K, Vendr-reported. 3. Bombora: The intent underneath the category Bombora is the topic-intent co-op that much of the ABM world resells, Company Surge data covering 17,210 topics, with contracts reported at $25K-100K per year. If what you actually want from 6sense is the intent signal, buying Bombora directly and feeding it into your own stack can be the cheaper, more flexible path. For the wider set, see intent signals . It is a data source rather than a platform. You bring the scoring, targeting, and outreach around it. Best for: teams that want topic-intent data to power their own systems instead of a full suite. Who should pick something else: teams that want scoring, targeting, and execution delivered, not just the raw intent feed. Pricing: $25K-100K/yr contracts. 4. Common Room: Community and product signals Common Room captures signals 6sense does not, community activity, product usage, and cross-source person-level stitching, starting at $2,500 per month. For product-led and community-driven companies, it reveals buying intent that account-level intent models miss. Zoom announced an agreement to acquire Common Room on July 2, 2026, which has not yet closed, so the post-merger roadmap is worth watching. It is signal intelligence, so it still needs an activation layer. The signals are strong; the outreach happens elsewhere. For how social media and other signals turn into outreach, see our guide to signal-based selling . Best for: product-led and community-driven teams that want signals beyond classic intent. Who should pick something else: teams that want signals to trigger automated outreach in the same tool, or that want certainty on the post-acquisition roadmap. Pricing: $2,500/mo entry. 5. ZoomInfo Intent: Intent inside the data giant If you already run ZoomInfo, its intent and Scoops data add buying signals on top of one of the deepest B2B contact datasets, with the broader platform reported from around $15K per year. Consolidating intent with your existing enrichment source is a real convenience. For the vendor field, see intent data providers . It is a data platform first, with execution as an add-on, and its contract terms are worth reading closely before you sign. Best for: existing ZoomInfo shops that want intent alongside their data. Who should pick something else: teams that want ABM scoring plus built-in outreach instead of data plus signals. Pricing: add-on to ZoomInfo contracts. 6. G2 Buyer Intent: Catching active software buyers G2 Buyer Intent identifies companies researching your category and competitors on the review site, a narrow but high-conviction signal, sold as custom pricing within G2 Marketing Solutions (commonly low-to-mid five figures annually). When someone is comparing you on a review page, they are close to a decision, and that is a signal worth acting on fast. The limit is right there in the name: it only sees buyers who research on G2 Buyer Intent's own platform. It is one signal, not an ABM strategy. Best for: teams that want to catch in-market software buyers at the review-and-compare stage. Who should pick something else: teams that need broad account coverage and the outreach handled. Pricing: custom within G2 Marketing Solutions, commonly low-to-mid five figures annually. What is the best enterprise alternative to 6sense? Artisan, and enterprise is exactly where the built-in-execution argument lands hardest. A large org running 6sense typically also runs a sequencer, a data provider, and a RevOps team to keep the models and lists current and to hand scored accounts to reps. Artisan collapses this into one platform: named-account targeting, signals, visitor identification, and outreach, operated centrally by sales ops for a large account executive (AE) team who never log in. CRM owner mapping routes outreach from the right rep's mailbox; do-not-contact enforcement spans email, domain, social media, and phone; escalation rules and an audit trail keep it governable. Artisan is SOC 2 Type II compliant with SSO, SAML, and role-based access on Enterprise plans, plus a forward-deployed strategist and dedicated customer success manager (CSM). Usage-based credits for Ava's work, with dialer seats billed separately, replace the fixed platform fee. How we chose these alternatives Four criteria. How much of the job the tool does, from scoring accounts to sending qualified outreach. Data and signal depth, judged on breadth of intent sources and realistic coverage instead of vendor headline numbers. Pricing transparency, where published figures and attributed contract ranges beat pure demo-gating. And deployment fit for large, governed sales orgs. Artisan ranks first because it owns targeting and execution together, and it keeps the honest note that a team wanting only a scoring-and-ads layer for an existing machine should weigh a pure ABM suite. Stay with 6sense if... Keep 6sense if you have a mature ABM operation, a dedicated ops team to run it, and an outreach machine you are happy with, and what you want is best-in-class predictive scoring and advertising to point it at the right accounts. 6sense is very strong at that, and ripping out a working intent-and-ads layer to chase consolidation is not always worth it. The case to move is when the contract cost, the implementation load, and the separate execution stack start to feel like three problems where one platform would do, or when you want the outreach to run itself off the signals instead of through a team. For the wider category, see our guides to the best buyer intent data and sales signal tools and the best B2B website visitor identification tools . FAQ What does 6sense actually do? 6sense is a predictive ABM platform. It models buying intent across accounts, scores which are in-market, and activates paid advertising to reach them, with contracts reported around a $62,820 median (Vendr-attributed). It is strongest at telling you who to target; the personalized outreach to those accounts is a separate execution layer you staff and tool. What is the best alternative to 6sense? Artisan, for teams that want ABM with the outreach built in. It builds named-account lists, watches signals including Bombora-powered topic intent, identifies visitors, and has Ava run personalized outreach across email, social media, and the dialer, all in one platform. You have the targeting and the execution together instead of a scoring suite plus a separate sender. For a related play, see how to find companies backed by specific investors . Is Artisan cheaper than 6sense? They price differently. 6sense contracts are reported around a $62,820 median and can pass $100K. Artisan prices Ava's work on usage-based credits, so you pay for the qualifying, enriching, personalizing, and sending she actually performs, with dialer seats and phone numbers billed separately. By consolidating account targeting, signals, visitor ID, and outreach it replaces several line items at once. See artisan.co/pricing for the model. Does Artisan do real account-based marketing, or just outbound? Real ABM. You define named-account lists and ICP filters, Ava monitors account-level signals and identifies visitors from those accounts, and she runs personalized outreach to the right contacts. Artisan owns both the targeting and the execution natively, which is why it does not hand ABM to a separate analytics suite. For defining your own triggers, see Custom AI signals: define any buying trigger and act on it . What is the best enterprise alternative to 6sense? Artisan. It runs account targeting, signals, visitor ID, and outreach centrally, so sales ops operates it for a large AE team with owner routing, cross-channel do-not-contact enforcement, escalation rules, and an audit trail. It is SOC 2 Type II compliant with SSO and role-based access on Enterprise plans, and usage-based credits for Ava's work avoid a fixed platform fee. How does 6sense compare to Demandbase? They are the two full-stack predictive ABM suites, close peers on intent modeling and advertising, with Demandbase contracts reported from roughly $24K to $165K per year, median around $68K (Vendr-attributed). Both share the same shape: excellent at scoring and ads, with outreach as a separate layer. Choose between them on data fit and advertising strength, and consider Artisan if you want the execution consolidated. Can I just buy the intent data without the whole platform? Yes. Bombora sells the Company Surge topic-intent co-op directly, reported at $25K-100K per year, and many teams feed it into their own stack instead of buying a full suite. Artisan uses Bombora-powered topic intent as one signal among many and pairs it with the outreach automatically, which the raw data feed does not do on its own.

title: Can You White-Label Customer Feedback Dashboards and Reports for Other Brands or Teams?
summary: Partially. Thematic ships a workspace logo and org details, but no color theming, custom domain, or per-brand identity. Here is what each surface carries.
body_text: A retail group with six banners wants each brand team to open a report that looks like their brand, not like a vendor's. A franchise network wants every location to see its own numbers and not the store down the road's. A shared services team wants to hand 40 business units something they'll actually read. All three ask roughly the same question, and all three use the same word for it. Partially, and the split matters. Thematic ships one workspace-level branding control: an admin can upload a logo and set the organization name, and that logo appears in the portal title bar and in emails. There's no color theming, no custom domain, and no per-brand logo. One workspace carries one logo. Anything past that is handled case by case rather than as a packaged offering, and the fastest route to a report carrying only your brand isn't a branding setting at all. It's moving the data into a surface you already own. "White-label" bundles at least four different asks, and in feedback analytics the branding half is usually the easier half. Below is what each surface actually carries today, the route where your brand is the only one on the page, and the part of the question that creates real exposure. "White-label" is four asks wearing one word Separate the asks before scoping anything. Vendors answer them very differently, and buyers rarely say which one they mean. Surface branding. A logo, a favicon, a browser tab title, and a color palette matching the recipient's brand. Identity removal. Taking the vendor's name off the interface, the help links, the exported files, and the notification emails. Address. Serving from a domain the customer owns, with share links and export downloads resolving there too. Per-tenant identity. Brand A and brand B carrying different identities from one deployment, without forking. Two related terms get used interchangeably and shouldn't be. Embedded analytics answers "where does it live," meaning inside an application rather than a separate tool. White-labeling answers "whose brand does it carry." The two are independent: a fully branded standalone portal isn't embedded, and an unbranded frame inside your own app is embedded but not white-labeled. Gartner Peer Insights' market definition of embedded analytics says nothing about branding at all. That's a fair sign the conflation belongs to buyers rather than to the category. Depth also decides the commercial shape. Logo and theme settings are usually configuration. Custom domains, sender identity, and per-tenant branding are usually provisioning plus a contract term. Looker's Private Label option has to be enabled by Google Cloud for your instance, with pricing through a sales conversation. Zoho Analytics documents its white-label BI as available on request, with the domain fixed at provisioning and changeable only by writing to support. In partner terminology, a white-label partner resells a vendor's complete standalone product under its own brand, while an OEM partner incorporates the technology as a component of its own. Neither is a settings toggle. What carries your brand in Thematic today Surface What carries your brand What doesn't Portal title bar Your uploaded logo and organization name The product interface itself, and the platform address Emails from the platform Your workspace logo The sender address; shared Answers send from a Thematic support address Exports (PowerPoint, PNG, CSV) Your filters, metadata, and data Export-level brand templating is not a configurable feature today Power BI and warehouse destinations Everything, because Thematic renders nothing there Nothing; you own the visualization layer Three limits worth stating plainly. The logo is set per workspace, so a group wanting a different logo per brand would need separate organizations, and organizations are a billing unit. There's no public sharing: link sharing is read-only inside the organization, and anyone opening a linked dashboard needs an account, though not a paid seat . And the regional addresses that exist (EU and ANZ) are data residency options, not branding ones. Where your brand is the only one on the page The cleanest answer to the branding question isn't a branding feature. It's moving the analysis into a surface you already control. Thematic ships a Power BI data connector, distributed as a .mez file for Power BI Desktop. It exposes themes as rows carrying name, count, base score, impact, and sentiment, navigable by organization, survey, and data source. Because it's a data connector rather than a visual embed, Thematic renders nothing. Your analysts build the report in your workbook, on your template, and the output carries your branding by default rather than by configuration. The same logic covers the warehouse route. Thematic supports recurring automated exports to SFTP, Snowflake, and BigQuery, per dataset and on a schedule, with configurable columns and full or changed-only modes, plus write-back to Microsoft Dynamics. Once themes and scores are rows in your warehouse, whatever your reporting layer draws is yours. The trade-off is worth naming. You're getting structured theme data, not a finished visualization. You inherit the design control and the design work at the same time. The half of the question that carries the real exposure For a multi-brand group, "can you white-label it" is usually standing in for something sharper: can I hand brand X a report that looks like brand X's and contains only brand X's data. Branding is the visible half. Permissions are the half that creates exposure. The governance principle from embedded analytics applies directly. Enforcement belongs at the data layer, not the presentation layer. A filter applied at query time based on who is asking, which the viewer cannot remove, is a permission. Hiding a chart is not. The canonical multi-unit requirement is simultaneous roll-up and isolation: corporate sees the whole network and can drill into any location, while each location sees only itself, usually for competitive-territory reasons. Roll-up only holds if the metric means the same thing in every brand, which is its own problem to solve . This is where Thematic is considerably stronger than it is on branding. Lens Views create tailored perspectives on one underlying Lens for different teams or regions without duplicating setup, and they carry always-on data restrictions that view users cannot disable, plus minimum row requirements. Each view gets its own shareable URL. Underneath, permissions run per dashboard and per dataset, with four default roles, custom per-user permissions, SAML 2.0 single sign-on, just-in-time provisioning, and System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) v2 for user lifecycle management. A perfectly branded dashboard that leaks a sibling brand's scores is a worse outcome than a plain one that doesn't. How multi-unit teams actually ship branded reports The working pattern is to generate the analysis in Thematic and deliver it inside your own template. Community Health System, a not-for-profit healthcare network serving California's central San Joaquin Valley, runs an annual employee engagement survey across 250 departments. Its Organizational Development team built one dashboard template in Thematic with the same layout for every department, applied a department filter, and copied the outputs into their own Canva template. That produced 250 one-page reports in a single three-day sprint. Preparation dropped from roughly an hour to about 20 minutes per department. The team saved more than 160 hours and over $10,000 per reporting cycle. "We were able to reach 250 departments," said Alexandra Clifton, Organizational Development Partner. "Yes, it was a lot of work, but it was all front-loaded to a single three days." Every recipient got a one-pager in the organization's own design system. Distribution can also stay in-platform when the audience is internal. Greyhound is the bus network operating across the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Its post-trip customer survey feedback reaches station managers, who check their own station's dashboard once or twice a week. "Thematic allows us to identify issues and distribute them to our station managers in real time," said Matthew Schoolfield, Manager for Commercial Analytics. "Before, when we sent the reports out, we were just hoping that people will read them, but had no way of telling." A multinational food and beverage producer with revenue over $10 billion and more than 20,000 employees runs self-service employee engagement insights across eight business units and hundreds of sites, saving $170,000, the equivalent of 180 hours a month. Mitre 10 covers 84 stores and 20,000 verbatim comments a month with a three-person insights team. Two mechanics make the pattern repeatable. Dashboards can be downloaded as templates and recreated in another portal through a mapping wizard, which is how one layout gets stood up across many brands or business units. And email digests go to a subscriber list weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually, skipping any cycle where no new data has loaded. Questions worth putting to any feedback analytics vendor Is branding set per workspace or per brand? If per workspace, how many do we need, and how are they priced? Does our branding survive into exported files and scheduled emails, or does it stop at the interface? Can a recipient open the report without an account on your platform? If there's a custom domain, do share links and export downloads resolve there too, or do they leak the vendor host? Which of these is configuration we control, and which needs provisioning and a contract term? Can two brands carry different identities in one deployment without standing up separate instances? So, can you white-label it? Partially, and precisely. Thematic gives you a workspace logo and organization details that show in the portal and in emails. It does not give you color theming, a custom domain, per-brand identities, or vendor-name removal, and export-level brand templating is not a configurable feature today. Anything beyond the workspace logo is handled case by case rather than bought off a page. If the requirement is that the finished artifact carries only your brand, the shipped route is the Power BI connector or a warehouse export into a surface you already own. And the question to settle before any of it is not whose logo sits in the corner. It's which rows each recipient is allowed to see.

title: Masaje tailandés: qué es, beneficios y por qué todos hablan de esta técnica
summary: Descubre qué es el masaje tailandés, sus beneficios, para qué sirve y en qué se diferencia de otros tipos de masajes. ¿Es para ti?
body_text: Presiones profundas, estiramientos, movimientos asistidos y una sesión que se parece poco al masaje tradicional que probablemente tienes en mente. El masaje tailandés lleva siglos practicándose, pero hoy vuelve a despertar curiosidad entre quienes buscan nuevas formas de relajarse, trabajar la movilidad y conectar con su cuerpo. También conocido como Thai Massage , esta técnica originaria de Tailandia tiene una particularidad: no consiste simplemente en acostarte mientras el terapeuta realiza movimientos sobre tu espalda. Aquí hay estiramientos, cambios de posición y un trabajo corporal mucho más dinámico. Entonces, ¿qué es el masaje tailandés?, ¿para qué sirve y cuáles son sus beneficios? Te contamos todo lo que necesitas saber antes de probar esta técnica. ¿Qué es el masaje tailandés? El masaje tailandés tradicional, también conocido como Nuad Thai , es una práctica corporal originaria de Tailandia que combina presiones, movilizaciones y estiramientos asistidos . A diferencia de otros tipos de masajes, tradicionalmente se realiza sobre una colchoneta o superficie firme y la persona permanece vestida con ropa cómoda que permita moverse libremente. Otra diferencia importante es que normalmente no utiliza aceites como ocurre en muchas técnicas de masaje relajante. Durante la sesión, el terapeuta puede utilizar sus manos, pulgares, antebrazos, codos, rodillas e incluso pies para realizar diferentes presiones y guiar el cuerpo a través de distintas posiciones. Por sus estiramientos y movimientos asistidos, algunas personas lo describen informalmente como una especie de “yoga asistido” , aunque se trata de prácticas diferentes. ‍ ¿Cómo es una sesión de Thai Massage? Si estás acostumbrada a los masajes tradicionales, probablemente una sesión de Thai Massage te sorprenda. En lugar de permanecer completamente inmóvil durante todo el tratamiento, el terapeuta puede mover suavemente tus brazos, piernas y torso para realizar diferentes estiramientos. Una sesión puede combinar: Presiones rítmicas. Estiramientos asistidos. Movilización de brazos y piernas. Trabajo sobre diferentes grupos musculares. Cambios de posición. Técnicas de respiración y relajación. La intensidad puede variar dependiendo de la técnica utilizada, de la movilidad de cada persona y de la experiencia del profesional. Por eso, como en cualquier masaje, la comunicación es fundamental: si una presión o un estiramiento resulta incómodo, siempre debes comunicarlo. ‍ Masaje tailandés: beneficios que explican su popularidad Una de las razones por las que esta técnica genera tanto interés es precisamente su combinación entre masaje, movimiento y estiramiento. Aunque la experiencia puede variar de una persona a otra, estos son algunos de los beneficios asociados al masaje tailandés . 1. Favorece la relajación Aunque es una técnica más activa que un masaje relajante tradicional, sus movimientos rítmicos y el trabajo corporal pueden ayudar a generar una sensación de relajación y bienestar. Es una forma diferente de hacer una pausa y dedicar un momento exclusivamente al cuerpo. 2. Trabaja la flexibilidad Los estiramientos asistidos permiten movilizar diferentes grupos musculares y articulaciones. Por eso, quienes disfrutan actividades como yoga, pilates o entrenamiento de movilidad pueden encontrar especialmente interesante este tipo de masaje. 3. Ayuda a disminuir la sensación de rigidez Horas frente a la computadora, largos trayectos en auto o simplemente una rutina sedentaria pueden hacer que el cuerpo se sienta rígido. El masaje de estiramiento característico de la técnica tailandesa busca movilizar diferentes zonas del cuerpo mediante movimientos controlados. 4. Promueve la movilidad corporal El Thai Massage no se concentra únicamente en una zona específica. Los movimientos y estiramientos pueden involucrar piernas, brazos, espalda, hombros y otras áreas, convirtiéndolo en una experiencia corporal integral. 5. Puede ayudar a liberar tensión acumulada Cuello rígido, hombros cargados, espalda tensa... nuestro cuerpo muchas veces refleja el ritmo de nuestra rutina. Las presiones y movilizaciones propias del masaje pueden contribuir a generar una sensación de alivio y relajación muscular. ‍ 6. Es una experiencia de bienestar diferente No todos buscamos lo mismo cuando reservamos un masaje. Hay quienes quieren desconectarse completamente y quienes prefieren sentir que su cuerpo se mueve y trabaja durante la sesión. Para este segundo grupo, el masaje tailandés puede resultar una experiencia especialmente atractiva. ¿Para qué sirve el masaje tailandés? Más que pensar en el masaje tailandés como una solución para un problema específico, es mejor entenderlo como una técnica de bienestar corporal. Muchas personas lo eligen cuando buscan: Relajarse. Trabajar la movilidad. Realizar estiramientos asistidos. Reducir la sensación de rigidez. Liberar tensión muscular. Incorporar un momento de autocuidado a su rutina. La experiencia, sin embargo, dependerá de cada persona y de sus necesidades particulares. Masaje tailandés vs. masaje relajante: ¿cuál es la diferencia? Esta es probablemente una de las preguntas más comunes. Aunque ambos pertenecen al universo del bienestar, la experiencia puede ser muy distinta. Masaje tailandés Es más dinámico y combina presiones con movilizaciones y estiramientos. Tradicionalmente se realiza con ropa cómoda y sin aceites. Masaje relajante Suele realizarse sobre una camilla y utiliza movimientos suaves y fluidos, frecuentemente acompañados de aceites. Su objetivo principal es favorecer una experiencia de descanso y relajación. Entonces, ¿masaje tailandés o masaje relajante? Depende de lo que busques. Si quieres una experiencia activa con estiramientos y movilidad, el masaje tailandés puede interesarte. Si lo que quieres es cerrar los ojos, bajar el ritmo y disfrutar de movimientos suaves mientras desconectas de tu rutina, probablemente prefieras un masaje relajante. ¿Masaje tailandés o masaje descontracturante? También es fácil confundirlos, pero tienen enfoques diferentes. El masaje descontracturante suele concentrarse en trabajar zonas donde existe mayor tensión muscular, como espalda, cuello u hombros. El masaje tailandés, en cambio, tiene un enfoque corporal más amplio y combina presiones con movimientos y estiramientos. Si sientes especialmente cargada alguna zona de tu cuerpo después de trabajar, entrenar o pasar muchas horas en la misma posición, puede ser conveniente explorar qué tipo de masaje responde mejor a lo que necesitas. ¿El masaje tailandés duele? El masaje tailandés puede sentirse más intenso que otras técnicas debido a las presiones y estiramientos, pero intensidad no debería ser sinónimo de dolor. La experiencia debe adaptarse a la movilidad y sensibilidad de cada persona. Y algo importante: un masaje no es más efectivo simplemente porque duela más . Comunicarte con el terapeuta permite ajustar la intensidad y hacer que la experiencia resulte cómoda. ¿Qué ropa usar para un masaje tailandés? Otra de sus particularidades es que tradicionalmente no necesitas desvestirte. Lo recomendable es llevar prendas cómodas, holgadas o elásticas que permitan mover fácilmente brazos y piernas. Por ejemplo: Leggings cómodos. Pants deportivos. Playeras holgadas. Ropa deportiva flexible. Evita prendas demasiado ajustadas o que limiten el movimiento. ¿Quién debería consultar antes de recibir un masaje tailandés? Como esta técnica puede incluir presiones y estiramientos, no necesariamente es adecuada para todas las personas. Si estás embarazada, tienes una lesión reciente, atravesaste una cirugía, tienes problemas articulares o alguna condición médica que pueda verse afectada por la presión o los movimientos, es recomendable consultar previamente con un profesional de salud. También es importante comunicar cualquier situación relevante al terapeuta antes de comenzar la sesión. Masaje tailandés en México: ¿por qué despierta tanto interés? El bienestar dejó de ser algo reservado para una visita ocasional al spa. Cada vez incorporamos más experiencias de autocuidado a nuestra rutina y, con ello, crece también la curiosidad por descubrir diferentes tipos de masajes . Desde técnicas tradicionales como el masaje tailandés o el Lomi Lomi hasta opciones como masaje relajante, tejido profundo, reflexología o masaje deportivo, existe todo un universo por descubrir. Y no necesariamente tienes que elegir el masaje que está de moda. Lo importante es encontrar el que mejor responda a lo que tu cuerpo necesita en ese momento . ¿Qué tipo de masaje elegir? Antes de reservar, hazte una pregunta sencilla: ¿qué estoy buscando? Si quieres desconectarte y descansar, puedes elegir un masaje relajante. Si vienes de entrenar y buscas trabajar la recuperación corporal, quizá prefieras un masaje deportivo. Si tienes sensación de tensión localizada, podrías explorar opciones como el masaje descontracturante o de tejido profundo. Y si lo que despierta tu curiosidad son los estiramientos y una experiencia corporal más dinámica, ahora ya sabes por qué el masaje tailandés tiene tantos seguidores alrededor del mundo. No existe un único masaje perfecto para todos. Existe el masaje adecuado para lo que necesitas hoy . Tu momento de bienestar también puede llegar hasta tu casa ¿Tu cuerpo necesita una pausa? Descubre los diferentes tipos de masajes de Glitzi y encuentra el ideal para ti. No necesitas atravesar la ciudad, buscar estacionamiento ni volver a casa después de terminar tu sesión. Con un masaje a domicilio , la experiencia de relajación comienza y termina donde tú elijas. Agenda tu masaje profesional a domicilio con Glitzi y disfruta de una experiencia de bienestar sin salir de casa.

title: 10 Hero Cars of Group B Rallying
summary: If you watch archive footage of Group B rallying today, it’s enough to make you wonder how on Earth it was ever allowed in the first place: screaming, turbocharged four-wheel-drive cars with a vague appearance of something in your local showroom, blasting through forest stages or around tight mountain passes, with spectators just inches away, […]
body_text: If you watch archive footage of Group B rallying today, it’s enough to make you wonder how on Earth it was ever allowed in the first place: screaming, turbocharged four-wheel-drive cars with a vague appearance of something in your local showroom, blasting through forest stages or around tight mountain passes, with spectators just inches away, often throwing themselves into ditches or flocking into fields if the drivers got it wrong. Group B always seemed an accident waiting to happen, and unfortunately, that’s how it met a very abrupt end. Following a series of tragic accidents that highlighted the series’ dangers, the final straw came when Henri Toivonen and co-driver Sergio Cresto were killed on the Tour de Corse in a Lancia Delta S4. Nobody knows whether it was mechanical failure, a misread pace note, or driver error, but the Lancia appeared to miss a turn completely and launch itself off a cliffside, ending up in a fireball on the side of a mountain. Harrowing scenes, and with increasing pressure from teams, drivers, and the public, the FIA made the decision to ban Group B cars from the World Rally Championship at the end of the 1986 season. It was an awful end to an incredible era. Renowned for its daring drivers, ground-breaking technology, and extreme cars, Group B made its debut in the World Rally Championship in 1982, following the introduction of new regulations by the FIA. These rules were designed to encourage innovation, allowing manufacturers to create highly advanced vehicles with fewer restrictions on design and production numbers. The minimum production requirement was set at just 200 homologation units, enabling manufacturers to push the boundaries. Cars featured lightweight composite materials, turbocharging, and advanced four-wheel-drive systems, which resulted in machines that were insanely quick and agile. These were 10 of the most memorable Group B cars, even if a couple never even made it to the start line… Audi Sport Quattro Audi The Audi Sport Quattro was a pioneer of Group B, introducing four-wheel drive and turbocharging to the sport. Its short wheelbase and powerful 2.1-liter five-cylinder engine made it agile and incredibly fast on all surfaces. Audi’s relentless development helped secure multiple wins, changing the face of rallying forever. The Sport Quattro’s influence can still be seen in modern rally cars, and its distinctive boxy design remains an icon. Lancia 037 Rallye Lancia The Lancia 037 Rallye was the last rear-wheel-drive car to win the World Rally Championship, in 1983. Powered by a supercharged four-cylinder engine and loosely based on the Beta, the 037 was lightweight, responsive, and was particularly rapid on tarmac stages. It also happens to be, in our eyes, one of the most visually stunning cars of all time. Peugeot 205 T16 PSA Almost from nowhere, the Peugeot 205 T16 transformed Group B rallying. It was the first to use a mid-engine layout, despite its visual similarities to a front-engine showroom hatchback. Turbocharged and four-wheel drive, it delivered more than 400 horsepower and dominated the championship from its first season, winning back-to-back titles in 1985 and 1986. MG Metro 6R4 MG The MG Metro 6R4 was the smallest car of the Group B era and used a mid-mounted 3.0-liter V-6 engine that was naturally aspirated, unlike most of its rivals. It had a four-wheel-drive system mounted into a tubular spaceframe chassis and was recognizably a Metro, just like your British granny’s shopping car. While turbocharged rivals fared better on tarmac, the 6R4’s nimble dimensions, all-wheel grip, and smooth power delivery made it a forest favorite. Ford RS200 Ford The Ford RS200 was designed specifically for Group B and didn’t resemble any factory Ford car, though the windshield and doors came from the Sierra. It used a mid-mounted turbocharged engine making 444 hp. Its lightweight composite construction, incredible chassis, and four-wheel-drive system allowed for exceptional handling and acceleration. It was ambitious, and prototype testing began during the 1986 season, where it was clearly competitive—but it never got a chance to shine, as the category was canned before its first season. Opel Manta B400 LAT Images Although never a championship contender, the Opel Manta B400 must take the spoils for being one of the best-looking rally cars of all time. Unlike most Group B models, it also retained the bodyshell of the road car on which it was based. It used a 2.4-liter engine tuned by Cosworth to develop 255 hp, and while it lacked the outright power of its turbocharged rivals, the Manta’s rear-wheel drive and linear power delivery made it a hero on gravel stages—and always good for a photograph! Lancia Delta S4 National Motor Museum The Lancia Delta S4 was a technological marvel, featuring both a supercharger and a turbocharger, which gave it explosive power delivery. Its advanced four-wheel-drive system and lightweight construction made it one of the fastest and most sophisticated cars in Group B, pushing the boundaries of rally engineering so far that it ended up being tragically associated with the series’ demise. It was arguably the ultimate Group B car—but was it a step too far? Porsche 959 Porsche The Porsche 959 was developed with Group B regulations in mind, blending cutting-edge technology with iconic Porsche styling. Its twin-turbocharged engine, all-wheel drive, and advanced electronics were all focused on the series, but just as it appeared, Group B ended. So Porsche reengineered the 959 for endurance racing instead, notably the Paris-Dakar, with the French team of René Metge and Dominique Lemoyne dominating the 1986 event. Ferrari 288 GTO Evo Flickr/Luca Rocchi The stunning Ferrari 288 GTO Evo was the Prancing Horse’s ambitious attempt to enter Group B and was based on the 288 GTO road car. Equipped with a twin-turbocharged V-8 and lightweight fiberglass bodywork, which influenced the shift from steel bodies on its road cars, the GTO Evo showed huge promise. But the project was halted before it could compete, leaving the car as a tantalizing “what if” in rally history. Citroën BX TC Evolution Citroën The Citroën BX TC Evolution was the French carmaker’s entry into the Group B category, built on the BX platform, but with extensive modifications. Featuring a turbocharged engine and hydropneumatic suspension, the BX TC Evolution was a fascinating and intriguing car, but not a massively competitive one, and with no notable results. Looks wild though, doesn’t it? The post 10 Hero Cars of Group B Rallying appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: Hydra Account Networks: How 20,000 Accounts Become One Actor
summary: Coordinated account networks defeat per-account review by design. How biometric, device and network linking collapses thousands of accounts into one actor.
body_text: Back to blog Blog · August 4, 2026 Hydra Account Networks: How 20,000 Accounts Become One Actor Cut off one account and two more appear. Hydra networks beat per-account review by design. Here is how cross-account linking — face, device, IP, email, phone — collapses thousands of accounts into a single resolvable actor. By Didit · August 4, 2026 · Updated Aug 4, 2026 The most useful number in Anthropic's February 2026 report on distillation attacks is not the 16 million exchanges or the roughly 24,000 fraudulent accounts. It is this: "a single proxy network managed more than 20,000 fraudulent accounts simultaneously." Simultaneously. Twenty thousand accounts, alive at the same time, under one operator. That is a hydra network, and it is a specific adversary design — not sloppiness, not opportunism, but an architecture built explicitly to survive the defense it expects to meet. Understanding why it works is the prerequisite to breaking it, because the failure it exploits is not a missing rule or a badly tuned threshold. It is a category error in what the defense is measuring. Key takeaways A hydra network spreads one campaign across thousands of accounts so that no individual account exceeds any per-account threshold. Lowering thresholds does not help. The attacker simply adds accounts — the cheapest input in the system. The signals that expose these networks are relational : shared devices, shared networks, shared payment methods, shared timing, shared biometrics. A per-account verdict cannot produce them. Face Search 1:N links two accounts to one human being. Device and IP analysis links accounts to shared infrastructure. Together they collapse the account graph into an actor graph. The most valuable single code in this context is DEVICE_RECOVERED_HIGH_CONFIDENCE — a device that has been seen before, returning after a reset or reinstall. That is regeneration, caught at the door. Linking is not accusation. Duplicate signals are informational by default — you decide the policy. What a hydra network actually is Strip away the specifics and a hydra network has four properties. Horizontal distribution. The workload is divided so that each account's behavior sits comfortably inside normal. Anthropic described patterns that "suggested 'load balancing'" — which is exactly the right word. This is an infrastructure problem being solved with infrastructure thinking. Cheap regeneration. New accounts can be created faster than old ones are removed. Every removal is a rounding error against the supply. Shared substrate. Under the surface, the accounts run on a finite pool of real resources — devices, IP ranges, phone numbers, payment instruments, and in many cases a small number of actual human beings completing whatever checks exist. Behavioral homogeneity. Because one operator drives them all, the accounts converge. Anthropic observed "identical patterns, shared payment methods, and coordinated timing," and prompt variations arriving "tens of thousands of times across hundreds of coordinated accounts." The third property is the vulnerability. Distribution is cheap at the account layer and expensive at the physical layer. You can mint 20,000 email addresses for nothing. You cannot mint 20,000 human faces, 20,000 unmodified handsets, or 20,000 residential IP addresses in unrelated ranges without cost that scales. Every hydra network is narrower at the bottom than it is at the top. The whole game is measuring at the bottom. Why thresholds are the wrong instrument Consider a platform that flags any account exceeding 50,000 requests in a month with a concentrated query distribution. Reasonable rule. Against a single abusive account it works. Against an operator with 20,000 accounts, it means each account can make 2,500 requests without ever being looked at — 50 million requests, entirely under the radar. Drop the threshold to 5,000 and the operator moves to 250 requests per account and adds accounts if needed. Every reduction in the threshold costs you false positives on real developers and costs the attacker almost nothing. This is a losing exchange, and it loses for a structural reason: the threshold is denominated in the unit the attacker controls. The attacker chooses how many accounts to use. They do not choose how many faces they have, how many physical devices they own, or how many independent network paths they can reach. Move the measurement to a unit the attacker does not control and the economics invert. The linking primitives Four signal families do the collapsing. Each answers a different version of "have I seen this before?" Biometric — is this the same person? Face Search 1:N searches a face against every approved verification your application has already performed. It is free with Didit identity verification and returns in under two seconds. curl -X POST 'https://verification.didit.me/v3/face-search/' \ -H 'x-api-key: YOUR_API_KEY' \ -F 'user_image=@./selfie.jpg' \ -F 'search_type=most_similar' \ -F 'save_api_request=true' \ -F 'vendor_data=account-8842' The response wraps a singular face_search object — { request_id, face_search: { ... } } — carrying total_matches and a matches array, where each match includes session_id , similarity_percentage , vendor_data , verification_date and is_blocklisted . If the same operator verified 40 accounts with the same face, one call surfaces all 40 — with your own vendor_data on each, so you can map them straight back to account IDs. This runs automatically during liveness inside a verification session, so in the common case you get the signal without making a separate call at all. Device — is this the same machine? Device and IP analysis costs $0.03 and is included in the $0.33 verification bundle. The codes that matter for account multiplication: Warning What it tells you DUPLICATED_DEVICE_FINGERPRINT The same device is behind multiple verifications DEVICE_RECOVERED_HIGH_CONFIDENCE A device seen before, returning after a reset or reinstall DUPLICATED_IP_ADDRESS The same address is behind multiple verifications AUTOMATION_FRAMEWORK_DETECTED The client is scripted rather than human-driven DEVICE_EMULATOR_DETECTED An emulator, not a real handset DEVICE_ROOTED_OR_JAILBROKEN A compromised operating system DEVICE_RUNTIME_HOOKING_DETECTED Runtime instrumentation on the client DEVICE_APP_TAMPERED A modified application binary PRIVATE_NETWORK_DETECTED A private or anonymising network path COUNTRY_FROM_DOCUMENT_DOES_NOT_MATCH_COUNTRY_FROM_IP Document and network geography disagree DEVICE_RECOVERED_HIGH_CONFIDENCE deserves particular attention. Didit distinguishes a duplicated device from a recovered device — a device that reappears after being wiped, reset, or having the app reinstalled. Wiping the device is the standard move for an operator regenerating accounts after a ban. That code is the hydra's regeneration step, made visible. Contact — is this the same reachable identity? Email and phone verification ($0.03 for email; phone via SMS, WhatsApp, Telegram, RCS or voice) test whether a contact point is real and reachable rather than merely well-formed. Farmed accounts lean heavily on disposable addresses and recycled numbers. Phone values normalise to E.164, so the same number cannot hide behind formatting differences. Document — is this the same credential? Identity verification emits DUPLICATED_DOCUMENT when the same document is submitted again, and POSSIBLE_DUPLICATED_USER when a submission resolves to a person already in your verified set. Both catch accounts sharing a credential even when the face or the device differs — and POSSIBLE_DUPLICATED_USER is skipped when the document number is on your document allowlist, so known-good credentials do not generate noise. From account graph to actor graph Individually these are just warnings. Together they collapse a graph. Suppose your traffic layer flags account acct_7781 — concentrated queries against one capability, unusual timing. Per-account review gives you one verdict on one account. Instead, take the verification session behind that account and pivot: Face — search the session's face across your verified users. Twelve accounts share it. Device — the session carries DUPLICATED_DEVICE_FINGERPRINT . Nine more accounts share the device, four of which are not in the face set because a different person completed those checks. Network — DUPLICATED_IP_ADDRESS across a CIDR range pulls in another cluster. Contact — three of the newly surfaced accounts share a phone number in E.164 form. One flagged account has become a cluster of thirty-plus, discovered from a single alert, using signals that were already collected at onboarding. And you did not need to inspect a single prompt to get there. The traffic layer told you something is wrong here ; identity resolution told you how far it goes . Which is also the limit of what this does. Identity resolution does not prevent model extraction, and it does not detect it. It never sees your prompts. What it does is turn one alert into the full set of accounts behind it, and make the next account off the same face, device or network expensive to create. Model-level output controls and semantic traffic detection remain separate, necessary layers — and they stay yours. The rule that keeps this honest A link is not a verdict. Didit is deliberate about this. In Face Search, status is "Declined" only when a blocklist match is found. A pure duplicate match returns "Approved" with DUPLICATED_FACE in the warnings — informational. The dedupe policy is yours, not ours. That default is correct, because duplicates have innocent explanations. A developer with a personal account and a company account. A shared office network producing DUPLICATED_IP_ADDRESS for a dozen unrelated engineers. A family device. A university lab where twenty students verify from the same room. The right way to use links is as evidence that raises or lowers a decision you were already making , not as an automatic ban. Two accounts sharing a face is weak on its own. Twelve accounts sharing a face, a device, a network range and a query signature is not weak at all. Warning actions are configurable per code — a blocklist hit can force a decline while a recovered-device signal routes to review — so the escalation ladder is yours to set. Use cases AI API platforms correlating a traffic-layer alert to the full set of accounts an operator controls, instead of banning one and waiting for the next. Trial and credit abuse — free-tier farming uses identical mechanics. The same primitives that surface a distillation cluster surface a promo-abuse cluster. Marketplaces and gig platforms detecting sellers or couriers re-registering after removal. iGaming enforcing single-account rules and self-exclusion, where the same person returning under a new identity is the core compliance failure. Frequently asked questions Does this require storing biometric data? Face Search runs against the face index your application builds through prior verifications — sessions with save_api_request=true , or Passive Liveness with save_api_request=true . You control what enters the index and you control retention, in line with your own privacy notice and legal basis. If you do not enrol faces, 1:N search has nothing to search. What if the operator uses different people for each account? Then the biometric layer thins out and the device, network and contact layers carry the weight — which is exactly why linking uses several independent families rather than one. Paying real humans to complete checks is also the single most expensive way to farm accounts, which is the point: it moves the attacker onto costs that scale. How fast is a 1:N search? Sub-two-second response. It also runs automatically during liveness inside a verification session, so in most flows the linking signal arrives with the verification result. Won't this generate false positives on shared networks? DUPLICATED_IP_ADDRESS alone is a weak signal and should be treated that way — offices, universities and mobile carrier NAT all produce it legitimately. Weight it low, require corroboration from an independent family, and configure the action per code rather than declining on any single warning. Can I search a face that never went through a Didit verification? Yes. Face Search accepts any user_image (jpg, jpeg, png, tiff or webp, up to 5 MB — PDFs are not accepted) and searches it against your index. If no face is detected the call returns HTTP 400. Ready to get started? Cross-account linking is available on every Didit account — no separate product, no minimum. Read the docs — Face Search 1:N and the IP & Device Analysis warning catalogue . See the product — User Verification . Check the pricing — publicly listed : Face Search 1:N free, IP and device analysis $0.03, full verification bundle $0.33. Start free — business.didit.me , 500 KYC verifications a month at no cost. title: The Best Family Vehicles Under $35,000 in 2026
summary: You can still get a great family car for under $35k, and you don't have to compromise on meeting your family's needs. Here, CarGurus editors pick 10 new and used vehicles that fit that budget, taking safety, practicality, and comfort into consideration.
body_text: Finding the right family car often feels like a balancing act between space, safety, and budget. For many households, a $35,000 price cap represents a sweet spot that opens the door to a wide variety of capable vehicles without stretching the monthly budget too thin. Whether you are managing daily school drop-offs, weekend sports tournaments, or cross-country road trips, this price point offers access to modern safety features, comfortable cabins, and practical cargo solutions that make everyday life a little easier. The good news is that you don't have to compromise on your family's needs to stay within this budget. By considering both the new and used markets, you can choose from highly efficient hybrid crossovers, rugged all-wheel-drive (AWD) SUVs, and even spacious three-row haulers and minivans. While some brand-new models fit comfortably under the $35K mark, looking at gently used examples of larger or more premium vehicles can maximize your purchasing power, giving you the flexibility to find the perfect fit for your driveway. title: Can an AI agent have its own email address?
summary: Yes. An AI agent can provision and operate its own email address with no human in the loop. Not a borrowed human inbox, not a shared team alias, but a real deliverable inbox the agent owns. How it works and why it matters more at enterprise scale.
body_text: Yes. An AI agent can provision and operate its own email address with no human in the loop. Not a shared team alias, and not a human's mailbox it borrows over IMAP or the Gmail API, but a real, deliverable inbox the agent owns, sends from, receives to, and uses to sign up for services, collect verification codes, and prove who it is on the internet. With an inbox API built for agents, provisioning is one call. The agent gets a live address on a default or custom domain, its own stored message history, automatic threading on replies, and an identity anyone can write back to. Sign-ups, magic links, verification codes, and multi-turn conversations all work, which is the difference between an agent that can demo the first half of a task and one that can finish a real one. The mechanics are simple. The reason this matters more for enterprises running fleets of agents than for a hobbyist running one comes down to identity, audit, and offboarding at scale. TL;DR Short answer: Yes. One API call provisions it, with no human in the console. What "its own" means: Not a borrowed human mailbox, where every action attributes back to a person, and not a shared team alias, where identity and reputation pool into one box. An address only the agent holds keeps its history, reputation, and audit trail separate. What it unlocks: Finishing a sign-up instead of stalling on the verification code, holding a real thread with a vendor or customer, and leaving a timestamped record. Why it matters at scale: 68% of organizations cannot reliably tell agent activity from human activity, and 82% have found agents running that they did not know about. What does "its own" mean? Three setups get called "giving the agent email," and only the last one is the agent having an address that's actually its own. The first is the agent borrowing a human's inbox over IMAP or the Gmail API. It reads and sends as you. Every action looks like yours, the provider can flag the automation and lock the account, and "which agent did this?" only ever resolves to a person. The second is a shared team alias like ops@company.com that several agents and people all touch. It works as a queue and fails as an identity, because reputation, history, and accountability all pool into one box no one owns. The third is the agent holding an address that is only its own : research-agent@yourdomain.com, provisioned for that agent, with its own thread history, its own place in the sending reputation, and its own audit trail. Everything below is about that third case. Agent's own inbox vs. the alternatives Capability Agent's own inbox Borrowed human inbox (IMAP/Gmail) Send-first email API Distinct identity per agent Yes No, it acts as the human No inbound identity Receives replies, codes, magic links Yes Yes, mixed into a person's mail No Per-agent audit trail Yes No No Provisioned programmatically Yes Manual and fragile Not a concept Isolatable per tenant Yes No No Survives provider automation flags Yes Often not Not applicable What can an AI agent do with its own email address? An address isn't a convenience bolted onto a capable model. For an agent working out on the open internet, it's the thing that lets the model act instead of draft. It can hold its own accounts. Email is still the internet's root credential. Sign-ups, password resets, and recovery all resolve to an inbox. With its own address, an agent registers for the tools and services a task requires under its own name, not a human's borrowed login that breaks the moment two agents need the same account. It can finish a sign-up, not just start one. Most of the web assumes whoever is registering can receive a code, and an agent without an inbox stalls on that step. With its own inbox, the loop closes on its own: Submits the form. The agent registers on the service under its own address. Receives the verification email. The one-time code or magic link lands in the agent's own inbox, already stored and threaded. Reads the code and continues. The agent pulls the code or follows the link and completes the flow, with no human paged to copy-paste anything at 2 a.m. It can hold a real conversation. Live work means counterparties who will never install your tool: a vendor, a customer, a scheduling back-and-forth. Email reaches all of them, and a persistent inbox lets the agent keep the thread instead of firing a message into the void and losing the reply. It has a memory and a paper trail. The inbox keeps a durable, timestamped record of what the agent said and agreed to, which doubles as its working memory and, when someone asks later, the receipt. "AgentMail took email from the thing I worried most about to the thing I worried the least about." Garrett Scott, CEO, Pipedream Labs. How does an AI agent get its own email address? With an inbox API built for agents, provisioning is one call: from agentmail import AgentMail from agentmail.inboxes.types import CreateInboxRequest client = AgentMail(api_key="your_api_key") inbox = client.inboxes.create( request=CreateInboxRequest(client_id="research-agent-v1") ) client_id is an idempotency key. Call it again with the same value and you get the same inbox back rather than a second one, which matters when an agent restarts mid-task and re-runs its setup. The agent now has a live address on a default or custom domain and can send and read straight away: client.inboxes.messages.send( inbox_id=inbox.email, to=["vendor@example.com"], subject="Quote request", text="...", ) result = client.inboxes.messages.list(inbox_id=inbox.email) messages = result.messages One production detail matters the moment you're past a prototype: provisioning can be anchored to a human owner , so the agent's identity traces back to an accountable person even though no human clicked through a console to create it. That property is what turns an agent with an inbox into an agent with an inbox someone is responsible for, which is the version enterprises can deploy. Why does this matter more at enterprise scale? At hobby scale, an agent with an email address is a useful capability. At production scale it's a governance question, and the numbers say the gap is already open. In a Cloud Security Alliance and Aembit survey, 68% of organizations said they can't reliably tell agent activity apart from human activity, and a separate CSA study found 82% already had AI agents running in their environments that they didn't know were there. Governance, audit, and offboarding all depend on being able to address the agent, and none of that works if the agent doesn't have an address. Per-agent inboxes fix this at the addressing layer. An address names the agent, scopes what it can be reached about, and leaves a trail of what it did. Pair it with per-pod isolation for tenant data and per-tenant custom domains for sending reputation, and retiring an agent becomes a clean operation instead of a forensic one. Do you need one? If your agent only ever fires one-way notifications and nobody replies, you can skip all of this. If it has to sign up for something, receive a code, hold a conversation, or be one of many agents you're running, it needs an address of its own. At fleet scale, that own address is what makes the fleet auditable. AgentMail gives your agents real inboxes. Create inboxes via API. Send and receive Emails with 0 complexity. Free to start.
