title: Empty sandboxes break developer experience
summary: Learn how Docker Sandbox kits turn empty sandboxes into productive development environments with repeatable tooling, credentials, and configuration.
body_text: I work on Docker Sandboxes , so I spend a lot of time talking about isolation, microVMs, disposable filesystems, blast radii, all the good infrastructure things. But the Docker Sandboxes feature I keep reaching for in daily use is kits . Kits sound like a packaging detail until you try to use a sandbox for real work. An empty sandbox is a good boundary. It’s also (eventually) ephemeral and empty, and that combination means annoyance and repeated setup work. The agent gets a clean filesystem, a baseline restricted network, and a clean credentials environment. Then it immediately needs gcloud , Java, Maven, some internal CLI, your package registry credentials, and that one skill where you distilled the tacit knowledge your team accumulated for years. Kits are the escape hatch from that ritual. A kit lets you describe what the sandbox needs, how it should get it, what it may reach, and which credentials it can use, then apply that description when the sandbox starts. Empty means setup work The usual sandboxing story is security-shaped: put the risky thing behind a boundary and limit the blast radius. Developers rarely keep using tools because the architecture diagram has a nice boundary on it. They keep using tools when the workflow is less annoying than the alternative. A blank sandbox starts from a place developers rarely start from in practice. Real developer machines have: SDKs, package managers, cloud CLIs, shell setup, local credentials, project docs, cached tools, and configuration nobody wants to reconstruct from memory. Some of it is good engineering. Some of it is archaeology. Both affect whether the agent can complete the task. The failure is rarely dramatic. The agent spends a few minutes installing packages, hits a blocked registry, asks for an API key it should never see, and the sandbox starts to feel like the thing between you and the work. At that point, the developer has a choice: spend ten minutes preparing the isolated environment, or run the agent on the host and move on with their life. We all know which one will win. What is an sbx kit? The kits docs describe a kit as a spec.yaml plus optional files. The useful mental model is simpler: a kit is the contract between the sandbox and the tool you want available inside it. A kit can install tools: schemaVersion: "1" kind: mixin name: jq commands: install: - command: "apt-get update && apt-get install -y jq" That is the smallest version. Useful kits usually do more. They can drop files into /home/agent/ or the workspace, set non-secret environment variables, run startup commands, start background services, and add agent context to files such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md . They can also describe the outside world the sandbox is allowed to touch: network: allowedDomains: - api.example.com - "*.cdn.example.com" deniedDomains: - telemetry.example.com And they can connect credentials without copying real secrets into the microVM. The standard pattern keeps the credential on the host, gives the agent a sentinel value, and lets the sandbox proxy inject the real header only when the request goes to an approved service. network: allowedDomains: - api.example.com serviceDomains: api.example.com: my-service serviceAuth: my-service: headerName: Authorization valueFormat: "Bearer %s" credentials: sources: my-service: env: - MY_SERVICE_API_KEY environment: proxyManaged: # Agent sees "proxy-managed"; the host proxy injects the real token. - MY_SERVICE_API_KEY Inside the sandbox the agent sees MY_SERVICE_API_KEY=proxy-managed . The actual secret stays on the host. The proxy replaces the header on the way out. That distinction is why credential support belongs in the kit contract. If the sandbox exists to keep the agent away from host secrets, copying those secrets into the microVM would be a strange way to celebrate. Mixin kits are the norm There are two kit shapes in the spec. A kind: sandbox kit defines a full agent runtime: image, entrypoint, policy, the whole thing. Use that when you are building an agent. Most integrations should be mixins. A mixin kit extends an existing sandbox with one capability. It installs the tool, opens the narrow network path, wires credentials, and gives the agent enough instructions to use the thing. The runtime stays with the agent kit. That is the shape I use for most of my own kits. For example, the kits I keep using daily are agy , yt-transcript , and tessl . The YouTube kit is exactly what you think: give the sandbox the tools to fetch transcripts and media metadata without turning every new sandbox into a small dependency archaeology project. The Tessl kit is even more direct. It brings skills into the agent running inside the sandbox, so I do not need to inject them manually like a medieval peasant. The nice part of mixins is that they stack. A giant “Oleg’s entire laptop, but in a microVM” kit would be funny once and then become a maintenance incident. You want small kits with clear jobs: a Java kit that installs a JDK, Maven, SDKMAN!, team Maven settings, and links to Spring docs; a gcloud kit that installs the CLI, allows the right Google API domains, and wires credentials through the proxy; a Google Workspace kit that gives the agent access to your email and Google Docs; a Tessl kit that brings skills into the sandbox; a YouTube transcript kit that adds yt-dlp , ffmpeg , and whatever network access those need. Then a sandbox can be assembled for the task: sbx run claude . \ --kit docker.io/acme/sbx-java-kit:1.0 \ --kit docker.io/acme/sbx-gcloud-kit:1.0 \ --kit docker.io/acme/sbx-tessl-kit:1.0 The same agent now starts with a different contract around it. At that point kits stop being a packaging mechanism and start being a productivity feature. The sandbox stays disposable, but the setup becomes repeatable. The developer can throw away the environment without throwing away the knowledge of how to rebuild it. Sharing is caring Local setup scripts are fine until the second person needs them. At that point they become documentation, and documentation becomes stale with excellent punctuality. Then someone pastes a token into a config file because the happy path was missing. A kit gives that setup a place to live. Vendors can publish kits for their CLIs or APIs. Inside a company, the same pattern works for package registries, cloud accounts, corporate proxy certificates, and preferred language toolchains. The user gets one --kit flag instead of a wiki page and a feeling of mild dread. Distribution matters here. Kits support local directories, Git URLs, and OCI artifacts. For shared kits, OCI distribution is the obvious path because users can reference a versioned artifact directly: sbx run claude --kit docker.io/acme/sbx-my-product-kit:1.0 Keep the source in GitHub or wherever your team collaborates. Publish the artifact to Docker Hub or another OCI registry. The source repo is where people review, patch, and complain politely. The registry is what makes the kit easy to consume. All in all Security is a good reason to care about kits. The network and credential contract becomes explicit, which is useful by itself. The daily-use reason is more prosaic: kits make sandboxes survivable as a development tool. An empty sandbox is a boundary. A configured sandbox is a place where an agent can actually work. Kits are how that configuration becomes repeatable, reviewable, and shareable. The kits docs and examples are enough to build a first mixin kit without inventing the shape from scratch. Isolation only survives contact with developers when it is at least as convenient as skipping it.

title: How we’re helping build Alaska’s skilled trades workforce
summary: In Alaska, skilled trades power the economy, but businesses need more trained workers to keep growing. Wells Fargo is supporting local trades schools to strengthen the career pathways driving vital industries in the region.
body_text: Your Business August 18, 2026 | 6 min read How we’re helping build Alaska’s skilled trades workforce In Alaska, skilled trades power the economy, but businesses need more trained workers to keep growing. Wells Fargo is supporting local trades schools to strengthen the career pathways driving vital industries in the region. By Eric Best , Staff Writer Mike Rowe, a longtime champion of the skilled trades, worked alongside Wells Fargo to spotlight craftspeople across Alaska like the boatbuilders at Bay Weld Boats in Homer, Alaska. Key takeaways Why skilled trades need support: Government data shows a widening gap between the number of skilled tradespeople retiring and the number of new workers entering the trades to replace them. An economy built on skilled trades: This gap means skilled trades are in high demand, including in Alaska where businesses rely on new talent to sustain vital sectors of the economy. How we’re investing in workforce development: Two $250,000 donations from Wells Fargo are supporting skilled trades programs at the Alaska Vocational Technical Center (AVTEC) and the Fairbanks Pipeline Training Center (FPTC) to help foster the state’s future tradespeople. Within days of graduating, Allyson Chryss had what many students hope for: a good-paying, career-oriented job. In her field, this quick start is increasingly common. As a fabricator for Bay Weld Boats in Homer, Alaska, Chryss is part of a skilled trades workforce in high demand. One reason is a shrinking talent pool: For every five people aging out of the skilled trades, only two are entering the field, the U.S. Department of Education estimates . “I had an opportunity to work anywhere in the world, and I didn’t even make it out of Alaska,” she said. “What we do here really is art. … It’s just like a giant puzzle, and I get to go home every day knowing that I’m building this incredible thing.” Bay Weld Boats creates fully custom boats meant for whale watching, commercial fishing, and other Alaskan industries. For Bay Weld Boats, this talent gap directly limits business growth. That has a ripple effect. For Homer, a town of about 6,000 known as the world’s halibut fishing capital , that can mean fewer boats serving the commercial fishing, tourism, and marine industries that help drive the local economy. To help address this need, Wells Fargo is supporting the Alaska Vocational Technical Center (AVTEC) with a $250,000 donation to help grow its skilled trades programs and offer scholarships to the next generation of Alaska’s tradespeople. The support is part of Wells Fargo’s broader effort to help local businesses and communities build the workforce they need to grow. The state school has been an essential source of fresh talent for Bay Weld Boats, where 20% of the workforce is made up of AVTEC graduates, including Chryss. “It’s 100% vital to the business to have this kind of skill set available to not only sustain but grow the workforce,” said Eric Engebretsen, the company’s second-generation owner. “It’s the only way the business exists; it survives.” [Video overview: Through the voices of business owners, trainees, and industry leaders, this video explores the growing demand for skilled trades workers in Alaska. It showcases the role workforce training plays in helping people build rewarding careers and helping local businesses thrive.] [Music] [Mike Rowe, CEO, mikeroweWORKS Foundation] Every small business owner I ever talked to they all told me the same thing: Finding people who would show up early and stay late and master a useful skill. That was the single biggest challenge I heard every day for 20 years. And every time somebody told me about that challenge, I would say, ‘You ever been to Alaska? They get it. They know.’ [Eric Engebretsen, Owner and CEO, Bay Weld Boats] Our primary limitation at Bay Weld is workforce, the skilled people to do what we need to do. The only way we can produce custom aluminum boats, we have to have the highest skilled tradespeople anywhere. [Cory Ortiz, Division Director, Alaska Vocational Technical Center (AVTEC)] AVTECH is a post-secondary vocational training center. We really focus primarily on hands-on training. More students are recognizing that there’s a significant return on investment for doing skilled trades. [Alison Hawkins, Head of External Relations, Wells Fargo] We chatted a little bit about what his needs were and felt like investing in Alaska would be money well spent. So, we are, happy to announce a $250,000 donation to AVTECH. [Applause] [Sam Mazzeo, Commercial Banking Leader, Wells Fargo] Skilled labor, from electricians to welders to plumbers to carpenters. We need about 1,500 people in those trades every year right now. [Mike Dunleavy, Governor of Alaska] The best years for Alaska are the next 50 years. And you guys have been the ones that built Alaska. You will be the ones that build Alaska. And I just appreciate everything you do to build this great state. [Allison Chris, Welder, Bay Weld] My dad is a naval engineer, so I wanted to work with boats and learned that welding was really fun. [Amy Schumacher, Director, Fairbanks Pipeline Training Center] The whole reason FPTC was built was to bring the trades together, to train together, because you go to the slope and you work together, so you might as well train together first. We have a pipeline training and everybody gets together. We build a mock pipeline, everybody knows a little bit about everybody else’s job so that you can orientate yourself when you’re on the slope. [Rowe] What are the risks? Okay. Where’s the danger? [Danny Ruerup, Assistant Director, Alaska Laborers Training School] So, the danger is literally getting out of bed every day. You’re working in climates that are anywhere from zero to 75 below, 80 below. [Unidentified speaker] We’re loading up this truck here. [Unidentified speaker] You’re under control, right? [Rowe] I can’t believe they tossed me the keys to the crane. It’s unbelievable. [Music] [Dan Sullivan, U.S. Senator, Alaska] I never tire of bringing federal officials up here to see it. [Vern Miller, COO, ASRC Energy Services-Houston Contracting Company, Inc.] So, I think that these are important ways in which we can increase our skilled labor force. Without places like this, to train people to do this work, America falls apart. So America’s biggest resource is the people that’s in it. [Mary Knell, Vice Chair, Wells Fargo Commercial Banking] That is why today I’m very proud, on behalf of Wells Fargo, to announce a $250,000 philanthropic investment. [Whistling and applause] [Schumacher] We plan to update some of our equipment. We have a couple welders here, in fact, that we need to modernize. And, we will expand the introductory classes that some of our students take here at the Fairbanks Pipeline Training Center. [Rowe] All we can do with what we know in the moment that we’re in is tell the best stories we can, and the stories that we need to tell are right in front of us. They’re the graduates of your program. [Ruerup] I was going to explain to my wife, ‘I just quit my job.’ Found the laborers hall, signed up, and a week later I was on the job making three times more money than I’d ever made in my entire life. [Rowe] It’s the American dream. In Alaska, skilled trades power the economy, but local businesses like Bay Weld Boats need more trained workers to keep growing. Wells Fargo is supporting local trades schools like the Alaska Vocational Technical Center (AVTEC) and Fairbanks Pipeline Training Center (FPTC) to strengthen the career pathways driving vital industries in the region. (03:48) Why Alaska businesses need more skilled trades workers If you look out at the frigid waters of Kachemak Bay, you’ll see plenty of Bay Weld Boats’ custom aluminum vessels: fishing boats, research vessels, whale-watching tour boats, and everything in between. Many of those vessels would not be possible without AVTEC’s skilled trades programs in Seward, a few hours’ drive away. At the state’s top-ranked vocational school , these programs fill up in minutes. Supporting Alaska’s pipeline training Alaskan businesses serve a critical role in the country’s oil and gas industries. That work requires a constant supply of skilled workers, from welders and pipefitters to surveyors and electricians. That’s why Wells Fargo also donated $250,000 to the Fairbanks Pipeline Training Center (FPTC) to help its workforce training programs. The center is the country’s only multicraft training trust, which means students learning various skilled trades work alongside each other. That replicates a real pipeline work site. “If you want anything built, you’re going to have to have the trades come in and build them,” said Amy Schumacher, director of the FPTC. “Any of the workforce development we can invest in today is going to help us tomorrow.” Alaskan companies like Arctic Slope Regional Corporation (ASRC) and its subsidiaries rely on the FPTC and other training centers for tradespeople. “To keep this industry growing, we absolutely have to have a workforce. And to keep that workforce and train them, we have to have people reach out, find these people who want to get trained, and have a good place to get trained,” said Vernon Miller, a general superintendent for Houston Contracting, an ASRC subsidiary and the state’s largest union pipeline company. “America’s biggest resource is the people who are in it.” It’s not hard to understand why: 93% of AVTEC graduates find jobs. The school does not have enough capacity to meet demand, and Wells Fargo’s donation will also help support faculty. “Alaska’s economy runs on the skilled trades, and we see that reflected in our enrollment numbers right now. We have more students interested in training than we have training slots. It’s both a wonderful place to be and a difficult place because we desperately want to keep Alaskans in Alaskan jobs,” said Cory Ortiz, the school’s division director. For many Alaskans, AVTEC is the first formal introduction to industrial welding, plumbing, heating, and other trades. Those skills are critical for Bay Weld Boats because its vessels can include everything from kitchens and living spaces to high-tech computer systems. And because the business builds each custom boat from start to finish, Engebretsen said they need all this talent in-house. “Most of the jobs surrounding boat building come from experience and time in the industry,” said Brad Conley, general manager and COO of Bay Weld Boats. “To be able to give people a direct avenue to step into formal training that can line them up with a career with us is really important.” The business specializes in manufacturing durable boats that can withstand the extreme conditions of Alaska’s Arctic and Pacific waters. This region is crucial for many sectors of the economy. For example, Alaska is responsible for 60% of the country’s commercial seafood, most of which winds up in American restaurants or homes, according to the McKinley Research Group . Bay Weld Boats also serves the region’s popular sportfishing and ecotourism sectors. “A manufacturing business like this is creating a product that creates a service industry around it. … These boats go to work,” said Sam Mazzeo, Wells Fargo’s Commercial Banking leader in Alaska. “They are a mainsail for this community’s economy.” Wells Fargo donated a combined $500,000 to two Alaskan skilled trades programs, including the Alaska Vocational Technical Center, the only post-secondary career and technical training center owned and operated by the State of Alaska. How Wells Fargo is investing in Alaska’s future Wells Fargo has been banking and investing in communities across Alaska for more than a century, since 1916. That support continues in many forms today as the state grows. “There’s a tremendous amount of excitement here in the Alaska business environment,” said Mary Knell, Wells Fargo’s vice chair of Commercial Banking. “It’s a region that is investing in a lot of very important growth activities, such as infrastructure in energy, critical minerals, and developing additional resources.” Wells Fargo works with businesses and tribal organizations across Alaska to help them access capital for growth. Engebretsen has banked with Wells Fargo since childhood and is now working with Chris Vaughan, a Wells Fargo commercial loan officer and relationship manager based in Anchorage, Alaska, and the Commercial Banking team as Bay Weld Boats becomes a client. Engebretsen hopes Wells Fargo’s support will help bolster the talent pool that companies like his depend on. The potential impact of a larger workforce is huge. “If I had double the workforce today, I could double the business tomorrow,” he said. “There’s that much opportunity.” Tags: Education Funding Philanthropy Related Your Business stories Fraud and Scam Prevention Scam prevention after natural disasters 16 min read Read more Our Impact 5 big questions on quantum computing answered 6 min read Read more Your Business From basement beginnings to billion-dollar success 10 min read Read more B2B Insights ‘The logjam has broken’: Sponsors deal-making ramps up 15 min read Read more

title: Houston Proclaims August 18 "Cheniere Public Parks Impact Day"
body_text: In recognition of Cheniere and its employees for their longstanding commitment to revitalizing city parks and soccer fields, the City of Houston and Houston Parks and Recreation Department (HPARD) proclaimed Aug. 18, 2026, as “Cheniere Public Parks Impact Day.” Houston Mayor Pro Tem Martha Castex-Tatum presided over the proclamation during a City Hall ceremony attended by Zach Davis, Cheniere’s Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, and Wendy Craven, Director of Global Corporate Giving Programs for the company. “It is an honor to accept this proclamation from the City of Houston on behalf of every Cheniere employee for our longstanding support for and work to improve Houston parks and soccer fields,” Davis said. “We couldn’t do any of this without the Parks Department. We are just very proud of what we have accomplished over the last five years together, and we look forward to the next five years.” Cheniere’s partnership with HPARD commenced in 2021, and, since then, more than $600,000 and approximately 1,000 volunteer hours have been invested in park improvements to make recreational spaces safer, more enjoyable and accessible. Cheniere volunteers have revitalized 14 parks and co-hosted festivals and soccer clinics for hundreds of Houston-area youth. “Houston’s legacy in soccer and community recreation is strengthened through the long-standing collaboration with Cheniere, reflecting a deeply shared commitment to enriching public parks and providing inclusive, high-quality recreational spaces for future generations,” the proclamation reads. City of Houston District B Councilwoman Tarsha Jackson praised Cheniere and HPARD for their joint efforts on behalf of Houstonians. “We have been able to upgrade practically every park in District B through this partnership,” Jackson said. “Private-public partnerships are how we move our districts and our communities forward, so I just want to say thank you.”

title: How can you quantify the business impact of customer feedback?
summary: Quantify the business impact of customer feedback by measuring each theme's drag on a metric you already report, then converting that drag to money.
body_text: Most customer experience (CX) teams can describe what customers are unhappy about. Far fewer can say what it costs. In a Forrester survey of more than 300 CX professionals, 3 in 5 CX leaders struggled to link their metrics to business metrics, and return on investment (ROI) modeling was the least common skill on those teams. You quantify the business impact of customer feedback by measuring how much each theme moves a metric you already report, then converting that movement into money at a rate finance already accepts. Thematic does this with impact analysis . For every theme, it measures the gap between your overall average score and the average score of customers who mentioned that theme. That gap is the theme's point drag. Multiply it by the value of a point, or by the affected population and the cost per contact. The arithmetic is the easy half. The hard half is making the number survive a CFO who asks where it came from. TLDR Measure each theme's drag on a metric you report, then convert that drag to money at a rate finance accepts. Thematic's impact formula: Impact = overall average score minus the average score of customers mentioning the issue. Four methods cover most cases: score impact, cost to serve, revenue and churn, and analyst capacity. Mitre 10 quantified stock availability at half a net promoter score (NPS) point off its overall score. A number gets acted on only if it passes four tests: auditable lineage, a versioned taxonomy, valid comparability, and in-pipeline privacy controls. Don't sum per-theme impact. One comment can sit in several themes, so adding the drags double-counts. What "business impact of customer feedback" actually means Business impact is the measurable change in a business outcome you can attribute to a specific theme in what customers said. Not volume, and not sentiment. It breaks into four dimensions, and most programs measure only the first: Score impact. Points a theme pulls off NPS, customer satisfaction (CSAT), or customer effort score (CES). Cost impact. What the theme costs to service, in contacts, handling time, or returns. Revenue impact. Retained, expanded, or lost revenue attributable to the theme. Capacity impact. Analyst and manager hours spent producing the analysis itself. Executives fund against all four. CX teams usually report only the first. Volume and impact also routinely disagree, which is why Thematic's framing is blunt: volume lies, impact tells the truth. Four ways to quantify the impact of customer feedback Method The arithmetic Best for Where it breaks Score impact (point drag) Overall average score minus average score of customers mentioning the theme Ranking themes against a board metric Needs a score on every comment Cost to serve Affected contacts multiplied by fully loaded cost per contact Support cases where deflection is the goal Needs a cost per contact finance agrees to Revenue and churn Affected customers multiplied by churn delta multiplied by average value Cases that must clear a revenue threshold Backward loyalty data can overstate the economics Analyst capacity Hours saved multiplied by fully loaded hourly cost Proving the program pays for itself early Soft unless the hours are visibly reallocated Score impact is the fastest route, because the metric is already in the board pack. Bain's research gives the conversion its credibility: differences in relative competitive Net Promoter scores explain anywhere from 10% to 70% of the variation in subsequent revenue growth rates among direct competitors. Forrester puts a figure on a single point: for a mass-market auto manufacturer, a one-point improvement in its CX Index can mean more than $1 billion in additional revenue. Revenue math carries the most risk. As McKinsey warns, building a business case solely on backward loyalty data may overinflate the economics. Thematic uses multi-label assignment, so one comment can belong to several themes. That's correct for analysis and wrong for addition. Sum the point drag of your top five themes and you double-count every comment appearing in more than one. Report themes individually. Never add the drags. Why a quantified number still gets rejected Producing the number isn't the same as getting it believed. In a 2016 KPMG survey of 2,165 executives, confidence in analytics bottomed out at 10% at the stage of measuring effectiveness. Forrester's 2026 predictions warn that budget pressure will lure 15% of teams into a death spiral by feeding metrics obsession, and that dashboards without context turn CX teams into replaceable reporting functions. What separates a funded number from a questioned one isn't precision. It's provenance. The International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) set that bar: a figure is verifiable when knowledgeable, independent observers can reach consensus that it's faithful. Feedback analytics is rarely held to that standard. The four tests a feedback-derived number has to pass Test 1: auditable lineage from comment to reported figure. An executive should be able to click a number on a slide and reach the verbatims behind it, with the theme assignment and calculation visible on the way. ISACA , the IT governance and audit body, names four pillars of proof for an AI audit trail: request origin, data lineage, control state, and temporal integrity. Output logging isn't enough, because auditors ask to see the control path behind the answer. Test 2: a versioned taxonomy. If the theme structure changes between reporting periods and nobody logs it, every trend line built on it is unreliable. A defensible program can state which version of the theme structure produced a number, what changed, and whether history was restated. Ask for the change log. Test 3: valid period-over-period comparability. The IASB puts it well: comparability is the goal, consistency helps to achieve that goal. Four things quietly break it: Channel mix. A quarter heavier on support tickets isn't comparable to the one before it. Volume. A theme at 2% of 500 comments isn't the same evidence as 2% of 50,000. Sampling and seasonality. Both move independently of anything you fixed. The model itself. Research on empirical studies with large language models documents that silent backend changes in commercial APIs shift outputs over time. If your platform swapped models between quarters without telling you, part of your trend is the vendor's release notes. That is the trade-off in every feedback program: fresher analysis pulls against stable, comparable reporting. Say which one a number is built for. Test 4: privacy controls inside the pipeline, not bolted on. Masking of personal information has to happen before analysis, documented well enough for compliance to sign off. The regulatory floor just moved. Article 12 of the EU AI Act became applicable on 2 August 2026 and requires that high-risk AI systems allow for the automatic recording of events over the lifetime of the system. Gartner predicts that by 2028, 50% of organizations will adopt a zero-trust posture for data governance. How Thematic makes a feedback-derived number defensible Thematic calculates the impact, then shows the lineage behind it. Thematic's Score Change waterfall chart decomposes a period-over-period movement into the themes that caused it, and every theme is traceable to the mapped phrases and individual comments assigned to it. An analyst challenged on a number can open the evidence live. A market research program manager interviewed for the Forrester study put it plainly: "The transparency of the technology goes a long way in building trust with internal stakeholders." Thematic keeps the taxonomy under human governance. Themes are discovered bottom-up from the language customers use, which surfaces emerging issues at mention rates as low as 0.5%, then refined by experts in the Theme Editor. When themes are merged or renamed, Thematic re-analyzes existing feedback against the new structure, so the change doesn't silently invalidate the trend line it sits on. Thematic runs inside enterprise controls. Thematic is SOC 2 Type II certified and compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), with role-based access controls, an audit trail of user activity, and geographic hosting options. Personal information is redacted in preprocessing, not passed to language models. What this looks like in practice Mitre 10 attributed half an NPS point to one theme. The New Zealand hardware retailer runs 20,000 verbatim comments a month across 84 stores, and Thematic quantified stock availability as the drag on its score. Mark Vaughan, Head of Customer Insights at Mitre 10 New Zealand: "Being able to definitively state that improving stock availability would deliver measurable NPS improvements helped us reinforce this as a strategic priority." Community Health System turned analyst capacity into reach. The not-for-profit healthcare network serving California's central San Joaquin Valley used Thematic to analyze open-ended employee survey responses, delivering 250 department reports in a three-day sprint, saving more than 160 hours and roughly $10,000 per cycle. Before Thematic, formal deliverables reached only VPs. Forrester published its assumption. The 2023 Total Economic Impact study of Thematic found 543% ROI over three years for a composite $6 billion US e-commerce organization, including $651,629 of avoided manual data preparation and analysis over the same three years. Its largest benefit line, $1,788,360 of incremental income, was modeled on a 2% cut in cart abandonment in year one, growing 30% annually. That visible assumption is why the figure is auditable. A number you can argue with is one an executive can approve. A buyer's checklist for defensible impact measurement Ask these in the demo, not after the contract. Show me a number on a dashboard, then click through to the comments behind it. How is a theme's impact on a score calculated, and can I see the formula? Where is the taxonomy change log, and which version produced last quarter's figure? If we merge two themes today, what happens to the last four quarters of reporting? Which AI models are used, and how are we notified when they change? Where is personal information masked, and what evidence do you give compliance? What happens when a sample is too small to report on? Anything a vendor can't demo live is a gap you inherit. The short answer Measure each theme's drag on a metric you already report, then convert that drag into money at a rate finance accepts. Score impact, cost to serve, revenue and churn, and analyst capacity cover most cases. Then make it executive-ready: traceable to source comments, produced under a versioned taxonomy, honestly comparable period over period, and privacy-controlled inside the pipeline. Run one test this week. Take the largest number in your last feedback report and trace it back to ten individual customer comments. If you can't, the problem isn't your analysis. It's your lineage.

title: IonQ’s Space Division Awarded NRO Radar Commercial Augmentation Contract
summary: Award expands company’s national security portfolio and reinforces its role as a trusted provider of commercial SAR imagery and data services for U.S. government missions
body_text: Award expands company’s national security portfolio and reinforces its role as a trusted provider of commercial SAR imagery and data services for U.S. government missions COLLEGE PARK, Md. — Aug. 6, 2026 — IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading quantum platform company, today announced that Capella, an IonQ company, has been awarded a contract under the National Reconnaissance Office’s (NRO) Radar Commercial Augmentation (RCA) program. Under the contract, the company will provide commercial synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery and data services in support of U.S. national security missions. The award strengthens the company’s national security portfolio by expanding its commercial space capabilities and reinforcing its position as a trusted provider of advanced technologies for U.S. government customers. Capella provides all-weather, day-and-night high-resolution SAR imagery and data services that enable reliable Earth observation regardless of cloud cover or extreme conditions. “Our SAR capabilities are built for the mission demands of government customers who need reliable, timely intelligence in complex operating environments,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ. “This award reflects the continued trust in our commercial SAR platform, and our commitment to delivering advanced technologies that support U.S. national security.” Through the RCA program, Capella will provide commercial radar imagery and data services that help support operational awareness, mission planning and data-driven decision-making for national security users. The contract further validates the role of commercial SAR as an important source of persistent, resilient Earth observation for government missions. About IonQ IonQ, Inc. [NYSE: IONQ] is the world’s leading quantum platform and foundry - delivering integrated quantum solutions across computing, networking, sensing, and security. IonQ’s newest generation of quantum computers, the IonQ Tempo, is the latest in a line of cutting-edge systems. Earlier systems have helped customers and partners including Amazon Web Services, AstraZeneca, and NVIDIA achieve a 20x performance increase over previous quantum solutions and accelerate innovation in drug discovery, materials science, financial modeling, logistics, cybersecurity, and defense. In 2025, the company achieved 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity, setting a world record in quantum computing performance. Headquartered in College Park, Maryland, IonQ has operations in California, Colorado, Massachusetts, Tennessee, Washington, Italy, South Korea, Sweden, Switzerland, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Our quantum computing services are available through all major cloud providers, while we also meet the needs of networking and sensing customers across land, sea, air, and space. IonQ is making quantum platforms more accessible and impactful than ever before. Learn more at IonQ.com. IonQ Forward-Looking Statements This press release contains forward-looking statements. title: El Mundial de fútbol también se jugó en las plataformas de IA
summary: Durante el Mundial de la FIFA 2026 se registraron 14,3 millones de prompts relacionados con el torneo en las plataformas de inteligencia artificial (IA).
body_text: Durante el Mundial de la FIFA 2026 se registraron 14,3 millones de prompts relacionados con el torneo en las plataformas de inteligencia artificial (IA). En el entorno digital, los aficionados al fútbol recurren habitualmente a buscadores, medios deportivos o plataformas sociales para seguir la actualidad de los campeonatos. A estos canales se suma otro espacio de consulta, los asistentes de inteligencia artificial basados en modelos de lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM), donde los usuarios obtienen respuestas de forma conversacional. Desde el partido inaugural entre México y Sudáfrica (11 de junio 2026) hasta la final (19 de julio 2026), en la que España se proclamó campeona, analizamos la actividad registrada en las principales plataformas de IA* durante el Mundial. En ese periodo, se generaron 14,3 millones de prompts relacionados con el torneo, distribuidos en 9,7 millones de conversaciones realizadas por 5,5 millones de visitantes únicos. 1 Ampliando el periodo de análisis a las dos semanas previas al inicio del Mundial, observamos que la actividad en los asistentes de IA creció hasta alcanzar su punto máximo durante la fase de grupos, con 4,8 millones de conversaciones. A partir de entonces, el volumen descendió de forma progresiva, con un ligero repunte durante las semifinales y la final. En cuanto a la distribución geográfica de las conversaciones durante el torneo, Estados Unidos, uno de los tres países anfitriones, concentró el 15 % del total. Le siguió India, con un 13 %, mientras que Argentina, Brasil y México superaron cada uno el 5 %. Entre ellos, el caso de India resulta especialmente llamativo. A pesar de que su selección no se clasificó para el Mundial y de que el críquet es el deporte predominante, fue el segundo mercado con mayor volumen de conversaciones sobre el campeonato. Este comportamiento se enmarca en una tendencia más amplia que refleja el creciente interés por el fútbol en India. Ya a finales de 2025 registramos un impacto significativo en las redes sociales con motivo de la visita de Leo Messi al país, un fenómeno que analizamos en este informe elaborado junto a IAB SEA + India. En las plataformas de IA también detectamos el interés por los futbolistas. Tras analizar el impacto en las redes sociales de los jugadores que destacaron durante las semifinales —Leo Messi (Argentina), Lamine Yamal (España), Kylian Mbappé (Francia) y Harry Kane (Inglaterra)— en esta infografía , quisimos comprobar cómo evolucionó su presencia en los asistentes de IA durante la recta final del Mundial. La mayor parte de las conversaciones fueron en torno a los finalistas Messi y Yamal, con 137 mil y 41 mil respectivamente. A continuación Mbappé y Kane, con un volumen inferior a cinco cifras. El interés no se limitó a los jugadores que llegaron a las últimas fases del Mundial. El delantero noruego, Erling Haaland, por ejemplo, generó 79 mil conversaciones en las plataformas de IA y se hizo con 41 millones de nuevos seguidores en Instagram, Facebook, X y YouTube durante el campeonato. 2 Además, Haaland fue protagonista de numerosos memes creados por los aficionados. Él mismo reaccionó con humor a algunos de ellos en una publicación de Instagram que superó los 8 millones de interacciones. 3 View this post on Instagram A post shared by Erling Braut Haaland (@erling) El Mundial de la FIFA 2026 también refleja cómo las audiencias combinan las redes sociales y los asistentes de IA para descubrir, ampliar y contrastar información. Ambos canales están cada vez más conectados, ya que las respuestas generadas por la IA pueden recuperar y citar contenidos publicados en abierto en las plataformas sociales. Para marcas y medios, entender cómo las audiencias alternan entre ambos canales resulta cada vez más relevante. En nuestro próximo webinar The State of Social 2026, analizaremos desde una perspectiva cross-platform cómo convergen las redes y los entornos de IA, y qué implica esta evolución en el comportamiento de las audiencias digitales. Puedes registrarte aquí . ¿Qué significa todo esto para marcas y medios? Los grandes acontecimientos, como el Mundial de fútbol, ponen de relieve el valor de medir el comportamiento de las audiencias en todo el ecosistema digital. Más allá de identificar cuándo aumenta el interés o dónde se concentra la actividad, hoy también es posible analizar cómo utilizan los usuarios las plataformas de IA para explorar un tema, cuántos visitantes únicos mencionan una marca o un evento e incluso junto a qué competidores aparece o cómo evoluciona esa presencia a lo largo del tiempo. Integrar estos insights en una estrategia de medición cross-platform permite obtener una visión más completa de cómo las audiencias descubren, comparan y consumen contenidos en el entorno digital. Si quieres conocer mejor nuestra medición en entornos de IA y entender el valor que puede aportar a tu estrategia, contáctanos . Notas: - Conversaciones: número total de conversaciones registradas durante el periodo analizado. Cada conversación puede incluir uno o varios prompts. La métrica se calcula a nivel de conversación-día, por lo que una misma conversación que continúa en un día distinto se contabiliza como una nueva conversación. - Prompt: número total de prompts registrados durante el periodo analizado. title: Rolex Motorsports Reunion Class Spotlight: Bruce McLaren Trophy 1963-1974 Can-Am USRRC V-8s

body_text: There are plenty of exotic-sounding engines running during the Rolex Monterey Motorsports Reunion. The hills around WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca echo with wailing rotaries and tiny, turbocharged powerplants from more modern racers. Still, nothing sounds quite like a pushrod V-8 roaring with more than 800 horsepower. Even the “small” engines in this class start where the mighty 5.0-liter SCCA Trans-Am cars top out. We captured a couple of the qualifying sessions early in Monterey Car Week festivities. We also spoke to some of the drivers to get a feel for what it’s like to handle these unhinged racing machines at Laguna Seca. They’ll all be racing to capture the trophy on Saturday in case you need some motivation to make it to the track. 1971 McLaren M8E Brandan Gillogly This 1971 McLaren was campaigned by Frank Parkhill, who raced it at Donnybrooke in 1971 against Jackie Stewart, Denny Hulme, and Peter Revson, among others. Parkhill finished several laps down from those legends, but he did finish. After that Can-Am outing, it competed successfully in several SCCA events. Brandan Gillogly Brandan Gillogly Brandan Gillogly Brandan Gillogly Warren Briggs purchased the M8E with a big-block, but it wasn’t this mean machine from Jennings Engines. The high-compression big-block Chevy is now producing around 900 horsepower. “Boy, the corners come up quick in this, you know? What’s quite funny is the more you improve, the more you scare yourself,” said Briggs. “If I improve Turn Six—I’ve changed what I’m doing through there—all that happens is I arrive at the Corkscrew five miles an hour faster; it’s like, ‘bloody hell!’”. 1966 Elfin 400 Brandan Gillogly When Globe Products, an automotive casting company in Adelaide, Australia, wanted to show off its manufacturing prowess, it built this 1966 Elfin 400 and fitted it with a Ford small-block using a set of its four-cam, two-valve heads. The sanctioning body where it was racing, Confederation of Australian Motorsport, wasn’t happy that only a few teams were getting low-volume parts that weren’t actually in production. The exotic powerplants had to go. Mark Goldsmith explained that his car, the experimental quad-cam testbed, “went back to a 302 and went through a few owners and ended up in Tasmania.” Elfin founder Garrie Cooper bought the car and gave it a more wedge-shaped body in 1980, ditching its sleek curves. “It looked like a robber’s dog,” said Goldsmith (U.S. translation: It looked terrible). Brandan Gillogly Brandan Gillogly Brandan Gillogly Goldsmith had actually been in this car when he was a teenager. When he found it for sale in Tasmania, he could hardly contain himself. “Who would think 50 years later, I’d go and buy it?” Goldsmith wanted to return the car to its 1966 chassis, bodywork, and livery. That’s no small feat, but Goldsmith had reference material to spare. “We even have people who used to work for Elfin at the time. They took a camera to work and photographed the chassis building,” Goldsmith explained. The black-and-white photos provided enough detail to restore the chassis to its 1966 configuration. Brandan Gillogly “I went through the whole lot, from 2014 to 2018,” said Goldsmith. “That’s how it looked in 1966.” It even has the same Hewland gearbox, marked as the 38th LG 500 produced. Aside from the DOHC heads, it’s very much as it was when Globe raced it, and is virtually identical to how it would have been after the DOHC heads were banned. Its Ford 302 V-8 currently produces about 420 horsepower. “We’re so outclassed compared to these eight-liter monsters,” said Goldsmith, completely undeterred and loving every lap behind the wheel. Brandan Gillogly “We now race it all around Australia,” said Goldsmith, but this is its first time running in America. We asked his thoughts on Laguna Seca: “This is great,” Goldsmith replied, “There’s nothing like altitude in a racetrack.” With experience at tracks including Brands Hatch, Silverstone, Zandvoort, Monza, and Spa, he’s got opinions on what makes them memorable: “Never say to an Englishman that Silverstone is boring, because they get very upset,” he jokes. “Our favorite track in Australia, obviously, is Bathurst. It’s the Spa of Australia.” Goldsmith has raced at Bathurst several times and compares Laguna Seca favorably to his favorite track in his home country, with one corner reminding him of Spa. “The corkscrew is the Eau Rouge,” he added. We asked if the Corkscrew was scary the first time. “It’s scary every time!” He told us a racing buddy suggested that there are two lines through the Corkscrew, to which he said, “If there are two lines on that corner, I’ve used all nine of them!” 1966 Elfin 400 Brandan Gillogly Bill Hemming, from Melbourne, Australia, has owned his 1966 Elfin 400 for about 12 years. “I bought it as a box of bits,” said Hemming, “and we had to rebuild the whole thing, make a new chassis.” That was an awful lot of work, but Hemming has plenty of research material to reference as he’s the man who founded the Elfin Heritage Centre to keep the legacy of the Australian sports car manufacturer alive. The car had been powered by a Repco-Brabham engine, but it was damaged and needed a rebuild, and parts are tough to source. Now it’s using a V-8 that’s much easier to run and maintain, a small-block Chevy. “I had a spare Formula 5000 motor I put in so I could come over here,” said Hemming. “We’re a bit out of our league here. We’re running five-liter motors against the 8.4L McLarens, but that’s all right, someone’s got to do it.” Brandan Gillogly Brandan Gillogly Brandan Gillogly Brandan Gillogly The 302 is topped by Lucas fuel injection and produces about 500 horsepower. “It wants to be full throttle,” said Hemming, “which is a bit hard. I’m driving it like an automatic. I only use Third and Fourth gears around here.” The final drive gears in the transaxle aren’t a great match for Laguna Seca’s layout, but Hemming doesn’t mind one bit. “It is terrific. . . Every time I go around, I say, ‘oh, I could have gone faster there’, but you forget.” He’s having an absolute blast with a 500-hp, mid-engine missile; a few things would surely slip our minds as well. 1972 McLaren M8F Brandan Gillogly Chris Springer, from Los Gatos, California, was the man to beat in early qualifying, clocking in a 1:27.138 lap in his 1972 McLaren M8F. Springer purchased the car in England about three and a half years ago and shipped it to the US. It sat in a museum for nearly 15 years but spent plenty of time racing in Group 7. Springer speaks nonchalantly about the car’s monster big-block, “I don’t need to have, you know, a thousand horsepower,” said Springer. He estimates that the car may have had closer to 800 horsepower when the 8.2-liter big-block Chevy was new, but the mechanically fuel-injected engine breathes through intake trumpets without any air cleaners, so it ingests a lot more dust than a normal car, and consequently the bores wear much faster. He estimates the current powers at “seven something,” which Springer feels is appropriate. “You know, they say 720 to 740 is what they were in ‘72.” Brandan Gillogly When asked about his experience racing at Laguna Seca, Springer was quick to respond: “It’s the best ever,” he said, enthusiastically. “People don’t really recognize it, but Laguna Seca is all banked turns. Banked in your favor.” Springer didn’t just jump into a 700-hp mid-engine race car; he had plenty of experience running a Corvette, but found himself wanting more speed. “The first time I drove it (his McLaren), it was 10 seconds faster than my fastest Corvette. So it’s super fun, but, of course, you have to look further ahead, because you anticipate the next turn. There’s no rest.” 1970 McLaren M8D Brandan Gillogly 1970 McLaren M8D Brandan Gillogly 1972 McLaren M8FP Brandan Gillogly 1971 McLaren M8E/D Brandan Gillogly 1967 McLaren M6A Brandan Gillogly 970 McLaren M8C Brandan Gillogly 1974 Sting GW1 Brandan Gillogly 1971 McLaren M8E/D Brandan Gillogly 1970 McLaren M8C Brandan Gillogly 1969 Porsche 917 PA Brandan Gillogly 1969 Lola T163 Brandan Gillogly 1969 Lola T163 Brandan Gillogly 1967 McLaren M1C Brandan Gillogly 1967 McLaren M1C Brandan Gillogly 1967 McKee Mark 7 Brandan Gillogly 1967 McKee Mark 7 Brandan Gillogly 1967 Lola T70 Mk 3 Brandan Gillogly 1966 McLaren M1B Brandan Gillogly 1966 Lola T70 Brandan Gillogly 1965 McLaren M1A Brandan Gillogly The post Rolex Motorsports Reunion Class Spotlight: Bruce McLaren Trophy 1963-1974 Can-Am USRRC V-8s appeared first on Hagerty Media .
